Causal Learning with Invalid Instruments for High-dimensional Imaging Responses

Yiting Wang Note: Department of Statistics, University of Virginia.    Chunlin Li11footnotemark: 1 Note: Department of Statistics, Iowa State University.    Shan Yu11footnotemark: 1    Lily Wang Note: Department of Statistics, George Mason University.
Abstract

Large-scale neuroimaging studies provide high-dimensional imaging phenotypes for understanding brain-related diseases and their causal relations with biological risk factors. While instrumental variable (IV) methods can address unmeasured confounding in such observational data, existing IV methods face significant limitations when applied to high-dimensional imaging data, particularly in handling large-scale data and leveraging the intrinsic spatial structure of images. To address these challenges, we propose High-dimensional Functional-imaging Instrumental Variable Estimation (Hi-FIVE), a novel framework for estimating spatially varying causal effects when a majority of the candidate instruments may be locally invalid. We first establish identifiability conditions under which the spatial continuity of the causal effect surface propagates identification from regions where valid instruments form a plurality into regions where they do not, provided that invalid-IV effects switch on non-smoothly. Motivated by this result, Hi-FIVE combines penalized multivariate splines over triangulations for the causal surface and region-wise penalties for spatially localized invalid-IV effects, under an anchor constraint that keeps at least one relevant instrument valid on every simplex. A distributed algorithm parallelizes the computation over simplices for two- and three-dimensional images. We study the asymptotic properties of Hi-FIVE, establish consistency and pointwise asymptotic normality, and construct bootstrap-calibrated simultaneous confidence regions whose finite-sample coverage is evaluated through simulations. Hi-FIVE is illustrated with an analysis of the effect of phosphorylated tau on FDG-PET imaging in the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, interpreted under the stated IV assumptions.

Keywords: Causal identifiability; Spatially varying effect; Image-on-scalar regression; Imaging genetics; Two-stage least squares.

1 Introduction

Neuroimaging studies now routinely produce high-dimensional imaging phenotypes, such as structural and functional magnetic resonance imaging (sMRI/fMRI), positron emission tomography, and electroencephalography (EEG) (Ombao et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2023). These data offer rich spatially resolved measurements of brain structure and function and have become central to studies of brain development, aging, neurodegeneration, and neurological and psychiatric disorders (Wang et al., 2024). In Alzheimer’s disease (AD), for example, imaging phenotypes can help characterize spatial patterns of neurodegeneration and connect biological risk factors to downstream clinical impairment.

These phenotypes, however, pose a distinctive challenge for causal inference. Analyses of such data are predominantly predictive (Rahaman et al., 2021; Shen and Thompson, 2020) or associational (Yu et al., 2022). Such methods are useful for characterizing statistical relationships, but they do not distinguish correlation from causation and therefore may not reveal the biological mechanisms underlying genetic–imaging–clinical pathways (Siddiqi et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2023). Randomized controlled trials remain the gold standard for causal inference, but they are often infeasible or unethical in neuroscience applications (Weichwald and Peters, 2021). Consequently, causal analysis of imaging phenotypes must often rely on observational data, where unmeasured confounding can severely bias causal conclusions even after adjustment for measured covariates.

This article develops a causal learning framework for high-dimensional imaging responses under unmeasured confounding. The central idea is that the spatial structure of imaging outcomes serves not only to improve statistical efficiency, as in conventional functional data analysis, but also to strengthen causal identification. In particular, we show that spatial smoothness can help identify spatially varying causal effects in instrumental variable (IV) models even when standard pointwise IV identification conditions fail over substantial portions of an image. This distinction, exploiting spatial structure as a source of causal identification rather than merely a technique for denoising or smoothing, is the key motivation for the proposed approach.

1.1 Related Work and Challenges

Our approach builds on IV regression (Angrist et al., 1996), a widely used framework for addressing unmeasured confounding in causal inference (Kang et al., 2025). A valid IV must satisfy three core conditions: (V1) relevance, meaning that the IV is associated with the exposure; (V2) exclusion, meaning that the IV affects the outcome only through the exposure; and (V3) exogeneity, meaning that the IV is independent of unmeasured confounders. While relevance can often be empirically assessed, exclusion and exogeneity are typically unverifiable and fragile in applications.

This fragility is especially pronounced in Mendelian randomization (MR), where genetic variants such as single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) are commonly used as instruments. Genetic variants may violate exclusion or exogeneity through pleiotropy, where a variant affects multiple traits or biological pathways. In neuroimaging MR, this issue is amplified because imaging phenotypes are high-level biological outcomes that aggregate signals from multiple interacting systems. As a result, even genetic variants that are relevant to a scalar biological exposure may influence spatially resolved imaging outcomes through additional biological pathways not mediated by the exposure (Taschler et al., 2022). Classical IV estimators can be severely biased in the presence of such invalid instruments.

A large literature has developed robust IV and invalid-IV selection methods for scalar outcomes, often relying on the plurality hypothesis of valid instruments (Kang et al., 2016; Windmeijer et al., 2019; Windmeijer et al., 2021; Guo et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2022; Guo, 2023; Li et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024; Zilinskas et al., 2024; Lin et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2024). However, applying these scalar-outcome methods pixel by pixel to imaging data raises two difficulties. First, it requires the plurality condition to hold at every image location, an “everywhere plurality” requirement that is often unrealistic for neuroimaging outcomes. Second, it treats each pixel as an isolated causal problem and ignores the spatial organization of the image. Thus, pointwise robust IV methods fail not merely on efficiency grounds but also because they discard information that may be essential for causal identification.

A separate body of work treats imaging outcomes as functional data in image-on-scalar or function-on-scalar regression models (Zhu et al., 2014; Feng et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021; Zeng et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2024). These methods borrow strength across neighboring pixels, improve estimation of spatial signals, and provide interpretable effect maps with rigorous inference. Functional data analysis has also been studied in IV settings (Florens and Van Bellegem, 2015; Benatia et al., 2017; Cai et al., 2019; Seong and Seo, 2024; Petrovich et al., 2024). Existing functional IV methods, however, generally assume that all instruments are valid. They therefore do not address the central difficulty of imaging MR when most candidate instruments may be invalid. More importantly, existing functional approaches use spatial structure primarily for estimation and regularization, not for invalid-IV causal identification.

Scalability presents a further difficulty. Modern imaging datasets often contain thousands to millions of pixels or voxels per subject, with complex anatomical boundaries, spatial dependence, measurement noise, and structured local signals. Existing tensor regression and functional regression methods can be effective for small- to moderate-scale imaging studies (Zhou et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2021), but conventional functional regression techniques often become computationally prohibitive as image resolution increases. Thus, a useful causal inference framework for imaging outcomes must simultaneously achieve robust identification, spatial regularization, and scalable computation.

1.2 Our Contributions

In this article, we propose High-dimensional Functional-imaging Instrumental Variable Estimation (Hi-FIVE), a functional data analysis framework for estimating spatially varying causal effects when a majority of instruments may be invalid.

We first establish causal identifiability conditions for IV regression with imaging responses that relax the “everywhere-plurality” requirement of pointwise robust-IV methods. The key idea is a separation of smoothness classes: the causal effect surface is assumed to be CrC^{r}, whereas an instrument whose invalid effect switches on inside a region where plurality fails must do so non-smoothly. Under spatial identifiability conditions of Theorem 1, identification then propagates from the region where valid instruments form a plurality to the entire image domain. Thus, spatial structure contributes to causal identification rather than merely smoothing: pixelwise estimation followed by post-smoothing cannot recover the causal effect where pointwise plurality fails, whereas the joint spatial formulation can. Although our primary motivation is neuroimaging, the identifiability argument applies more broadly to function-valued outcomes.

Second, we develop an estimation procedure that operationalizes this identification strategy. Hi-FIVE models the causal effect as a smooth spatial function and represents it using multivariate penalized splines over triangulations. Triangulations are well suited for imaging data because they can accommodate irregular anatomical domains and complex boundaries (Yu et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021). To account for invalid instruments, Hi-FIVE introduces region-wise selection penalties that allow an IV to be valid in some spatial regions and invalid in others. This is important because different brain regions, tissue types, or image segments may be affected by different biological pathways. In addition, we introduce an anchor constraint that guarantees at least one relevant instrument remains valid on every simplex, mirroring the identification condition (A1) in Theorem 1. The resulting method estimates a smooth causal effect map while simultaneously identifying locally invalid IV effects. A key distinction from post-smoothing approaches (Fan and Zhang, 1999) is that Hi-FIVE uses spatial information during the invalid-IV selection and causal estimation steps. In non-causal image-on-scalar regression, one may estimate a coefficient surface pointwise and then smooth the estimates afterward. In causal imaging analysis, this logic breaks down: smoothing biased pointwise IV estimates does not restore identification when plurality fails locally. Hi-FIVE instead incorporates spatial structure directly into the causal identification and estimation problem, which enables consistent estimation under settings where pointwise robust IV methods and their post-smoothed variants may remain biased.

Third, we design Hi-FIVE to be computationally scalable for high-resolution imaging data through a domain decomposition scheme built on distributed learning for functional data regression (Yu et al., 2025). By partitioning the imaging domain into triangulated subregions containing relatively small number of pixels or voxels and associated local parameters, invalid-IV selection and effect estimation can be performed locally and in parallel, substantially reducing the computational burden. In particular, because the Bernstein–Bézier basis functions are supported on single simplices, the invalid-IV updates decouple across simplices, while the causal-effect update can be assembled from simplexwise quantities, so the algorithm parallelizes across workers with communication limited to shared-interface coefficients. The triangulation-based representation applies naturally to both 2D and 3D imaging domains, and the domain decomposition allows tuning parameters to adapt across subdomains, accommodating spatial heterogeneity in the underlying IV signals. Together, these features make Hi-FIVE suitable for statistically robust and computationally scalable analysis of high-resolution imaging data.

We then develop statistical inference for the spatially varying causal effect. Unlike classical variable-selection settings (Li et al., 2021), which typically assume sparsity among a large number of candidate variables, we allow invalid-IV effects to occupy nonvanishing portions of the spatial domain as the sample size increases. Furthermore, we accommodate spatially correlated observations through the error covariance structure and region-specific effective sample sizes. Building on the pointwise results, we construct simultaneous confidence regions (SCRs) by recalibrating the pointwise intervals with a wild bootstrap. These regions provide uncertainty quantification for the entire causal effect surface rather than isolated pointwise intervals, which is essential for interpretable inference in imaging studies.

Finally, we evaluate Hi-FIVE through simulation studies and an application to the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) dataset. The simulations compare Hi-FIVE with pointwise robust IV methods, post-smoothed pointwise estimators, highlighting the role of spatial information in invalid-IV causal learning. In the ADNI analysis, we study the causal effect of phosphorylated tau (p-tau) on FDG-PET imaging responses, illustrating how Hi-FIVE can estimate spatially varying causal effects while identifying region-specific invalid instruments.

The rest of this article is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the image-on-scalar IV model with invalid instruments, presents the spatial identifiability results, and describes the Hi-FIVE estimation procedure. Section 3 establishes the large-sample properties of Hi-FIVE and develops a bootstrap procedure for SCRs. Section 4 reports simulation studies, and Section 5 presents the ADNI application. Section 6 concludes with a discussion. Technical proofs, implementation details, and additional numerical results are provided in the Supplementary Material.

2.1 Causal Identifiability from Spatial Information

Because of endogeneity, the causal-effect function β∗​(⋅)\beta^{\ast}(\cdot) in (1) or (3) is generally non-identifiable from the observed data alone. Formally, non-identifiability implies that two different causal functions, β∗​(⋅)\beta^{\ast}(\cdot) and β~​(⋅)\widetilde{\beta}(\cdot), can be observationally equivalent, in the sense that, along with their respective nuisance parameters, both can generate the exact same probability distribution for the observed variables {Y⁡(𝒔),D,𝐙}\{Y(\bm{s}),D,\mathbf{Z}\}. Consequently, the data provide no basis for distinguishing between these two different causal functions.

Following Angrist et al. (1996), however, if an instrument ZℓZ_{\ell} is known to be a valid IV at location 𝒔\bm{s}, then β∗​(𝒔)\beta^{\ast}(\bm{s}) becomes identifiable. Specifically, a valid IV Zℓ{Z}_{\ell} at location 𝒔\bm{s} must satisfy three IV assumptions: (V1) Zℓ{Z}_{\ell} is (conditionally) associated with D{D}, i.e., γℓ∗≠0\gamma^{\ast}_{\ell}\neq 0; (V2) Zℓ{Z}_{\ell} does not directly affect the imaging outcome Y⁡(𝒔)Y(\bm{s}), i.e., ϕℓ∗​(𝒔)=0\phi^{\ast}_{\ell}(\bm{s})=0; and (V3) Zℓ{Z}_{\ell} is uncorrelated with the unmeasured confounders, i.e., φℓ∗​(𝒔)=0\varphi^{\ast}_{\ell}(\bm{s})=0.

In practice, the mechanisms underlying candidate instruments are rarely fully known, and it is often unclear which instruments are valid at which locations. Recent seminal work (Kang et al., 2016; Guo et al., 2018; Lin et al., 2024, etc.) has developed data-driven approaches to select valid IVs based on the conjecture that valid IVs are of plurality. To accommodate our setup, we formally introduce the following definition.

Definition 1.

For a fixed location 𝒔∈Ω\bm{s}\in\Omega, let 𝒱(𝒔)≡{ℓ:αℓ∗(𝒔)=0,γℓ∗≠0}\mathcal{V}(\bm{s})\equiv\{\ell:\alpha^{\ast}_{\ell}(\bm{s})=0,\ \gamma^{\ast}_{\ell}\neq 0\} denote the set of valid IVs at 𝒔\bm{s}. We say that the pointwise plurality condition holds at 𝒔\bm{s}, if

|𝒱(𝒔)|>maxc≠0|{ℓ:αℓ∗(𝒔)/γℓ∗=c,γℓ∗≠0}|.\displaystyle|\mathcal{V}(\bm{s})|>\max_{c\neq 0}|\{\ell:\alpha^{\ast}_{\ell}(\bm{s})/\gamma^{\ast}_{\ell}=c,\ \gamma^{\ast}_{\ell}\neq 0\}|. (4)

Further, we say that the everywhere plurality condition holds, if (4) holds for every 𝒔∈Ω\bm{s}\in\Omega.

When scalar robust-IV methods are applied pixelwise to imaging MR data, they require the everywhere plurality condition. This assumption is often unrealistic for imaging outcomes, which aggregate signals from multiple pathways and are therefore especially prone to pleiotropy (Taschler et al., 2022). This motivates new identifiability conditions for IV regression with imaging or functional responses that explicitly exploit spatial structure rather than treating each location as an isolated scalar outcome.

Functional responses, including imaging phenotypes, often exhibit intrinsic spatial structure, such as smoothness or local coherence, that can be exploited to improve causal identifiability. We next show how this structure can be used to identify the spatially varying causal effect β∗​(⋅)\beta^{\ast}(\cdot) by taking into account the spatial information in images while relaxing the everywhere plurality condition. To proceed, we introduce the following stability condition.

Otherwise, ZℓZ_{\ell} is said to be unstable.

Then β∗​(⋅)\beta^{\ast}(\cdot) is identifiable on Ω\Omega within the class of parameter pairs (β,𝛂)(\beta,\bm{\alpha}) that satisfy (3), β∈Cr​(Ω)\beta\in C^{r}(\Omega) and (A1)–(A3): any two such pairs that induce the same distribution of {Y⁡(⋅),D,𝐙}\{Y(\cdot),D,\mathbf{Z}\} have the same causal effect function. Theorem 1 establishes a new path to causal identifiability by using the spatial information inherent to functional data. As a result, it becomes possible to identify β∗​(⋅)\beta^{\ast}(\cdot) on Ω\Omega even if Ω0\Omega_{0} is much smaller than Ω\Omega. Theorem 1 can potentially be extended to a general domain and other functional-response settings.

Figure 1 provides an intuitive illustration of Theorem 1 with p=2p=2. The pointwise plurality condition fails in the gray non-plurality region, since with only two IVs there may be one valid IV at each location 𝒔\bm{s}, while for the rest of the region, (A2) is satisfied, since in this nonempty and open region, rℓ​(𝒔)=rk​(𝒔)r_{\ell}(\bm{s})=r_{k}(\bm{s}) for all ℓ,k∈ℐ\ell,k\in\mathcal{I}. At every boundary point of the non-plurality region, if α∗​(⋅)\alpha^{\ast}(\cdot) is CrC^{r} locally, then the corresponding IV ZℓZ_{\ell} is stable in a neighborhood of that point. Then (A3) is satisfied, and we can extend the identification to the non-plurality region. Therefore, the causal effect β∗​(𝒔)\beta^{\ast}(\bm{s}) is identifiable.

2.2 Finite-sample Estimation using Hi-FIVE

To estimate the spatially varying causal effect β⁡(⋅)\beta(\cdot), we construct a two-stage IV estimator tailored to imaging responses. Suppose we observe an independent sample: {Di,𝐙i,Yi(𝒔j):i=1,…,n,j=1,…,N}\{D_{i},\mathbf{Z}_{i},Y_{i}(\bm{s}_{j}):i=1,\ldots,n,\ j=1,\ldots,N\} from (1), where i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n indexes subjects, j=1,…,Nj=1,\ldots,N indexes spatial locations, 𝒔j\bm{s}_{j} denotes the jjth observed pixel or voxel location in Ω\Omega.

In the first stage, we project the exposure onto the candidate instruments by fitting Di=𝐙i⊤​𝜸+ξiD_{i}=\mathbf{Z}_{i}^{\top}\bm{\gamma}+\xi_{i}, i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n, yielding fitted exposure values D^i=𝐙i⊤​𝜸^\widehat{D}_{i}=\mathbf{Z}_{i}^{\top}\widehat{\bm{\gamma}}. In the second stage, the imaging response is modeled as a function of the fitted exposure and the candidate instruments, allowing the spatially varying causal effect β⁡(𝒔)\beta(\bm{s}) and the invalid-IV effect functions αℓ​(𝒔)\alpha_{\ell}(\bm{s}) to be estimated jointly.

The second-stage estimator is constructed using multivariate splines over triangulations. We therefore first introduce the triangulation and spline notation needed to define the penalized image-on-scalar regression criterion.

Triangulations provide an effective way to represent data distributed over irregular domains with complex boundaries (Lai and Wang, 2013). This approach is well suited for image processing, including both two- and three-dimensional brain modeling. Let κ∈{2,3}\kappa\in\{2,3\} denote the spatial dimension. We denote by TT a κ\kappa-simplex, that is, the convex hull of κ+1\kappa+1 affinely independent points. In particular, TT is a triangle when κ=2\kappa=2 and a tetrahedron when κ=3\kappa=3. A collection △=(T1,…,TK)\triangle=(T_{1},\ldots,T_{K}) of KK simplices is called a triangulation of Ω=⋃k=1KTk\Omega=\bigcup_{k=1}^{K}T_{k} if the intersection of any two simplices in △\triangle is either empty or a common lower-dimensional face, such as a vertex, an edge, or, in three dimensions, a triangular face.

For an integer r≥0r\geq 0, let Cr​(Ω)C^{r}(\Omega) be the space of all rrth continuously differentiable functions over Ω\Omega. Given a triangulation △\triangle, define the spline space of degree dd and smoothness rr as 𝒮dr(△)={s∈Cr(Ω):s|T∈𝒫d(T),T∈△},\mathcal{S}^{r}_{d}(\triangle)=\left\{s\in C^{r}(\Omega):s|_{T}\in\mathcal{P}_{d}(T),\ T\in\triangle\right\}, where s|Ts|_{T} denotes the polynomial piece of ss restricted to simplex TT, and 𝒫d​(T)\mathcal{P}_{d}(T) is the space of all polynomials on TT with total degree no greater than dd. We represent multivariate splines using Bernstein–Bézier basis polynomials on simplices. Let 𝐁⁡(𝒔)={Bm​(𝒔),m∈ℳ}⊤\mathbf{B}(\bm{s})=\{B_{m}(\bm{s}),m\in\mathcal{M}\}^{\top} denote the collection of Bernstein basis polynomials associated with 𝒮dr​(△)\mathcal{S}^{r}_{d}(\triangle). Then any function g∈𝒮dr​(△)g\in\mathcal{S}^{r}_{d}(\triangle) can be written as g⁡(𝒔)=𝐁⊤​(𝒔)​𝜽,subject to ​𝚽​𝜽=𝟎,g(\bm{s})=\mathbf{B}^{\top}(\bm{s})\bm{\theta},\penalty\ \text{subject to }\mathbf{\Phi}\bm{\theta}=\mathbf{0}, where 𝜽=(θm,m∈ℳ)⊤\bm{\theta}=(\theta_{m},m\in\mathcal{M})^{\top} is the spline coefficient vector. The matrix 𝚽\mathbf{\Phi} collects the smoothness constraints across shared interfaces of adjacent simplices (shared edges in 2D and shared triangular faces in 3D). Its dimension is J×|ℳ|J\times|\mathcal{M}|, where JJ depends on the triangulation structure and the smoothness order rr. See Zhou and Pan (2014) and Li et al. (2024) for examples of such constraint matrices.

To borrow information across neighboring pixels or voxels while accommodating spatially localized invalid-IV effects, we represent β⁡(⋅)\beta(\cdot) in 𝒮d1r1​(△1)\mathcal{S}^{r_{1}}_{d_{1}}(\triangle_{1}) and each αℓ​(⋅)\alpha_{\ell}(\cdot) in the broken polynomial space 𝒮d2−1(△2)={f:f|Tk∈𝒫d2(Tk),k=1,…,K2}.\mathcal{S}^{-1}_{d_{2}}(\triangle_{2})=\{f:f|_{T_{k}}\in\mathcal{P}_{d_{2}}(T_{k}),\ k=1,\ldots,K_{2}\}. The invalid-effect coefficients on different simplices are unconstrained, so jumps across their interfaces are allowed. Each observation on an interface is assigned to one adjacent simplex. The causal effect satisfies the continuity constraints defining 𝒮d1r1​(△1)\mathcal{S}^{r_{1}}_{d_{1}}(\triangle_{1}). For the theory, d1=d2=dd_{1}=d_{2}=d, r1=r≥0r_{1}=r\geq 0, and △2\triangle_{2} is a fixed-level refinement of △1\triangle_{1}.

The two penalty terms in (6) play distinct but complementary roles in causal identification. The roughness penalty on β⁡(𝐬)\beta(\mathbf{s}) exploits the spatial smoothness of the causal effect and favors a spatially regular causal-effect surface. In contrast, the region-wise sparsity penalty on αℓ​(𝐬)\alpha_{\ell}(\mathbf{s}) exploits the local validity/plurality structure of the IVs by identifying regions with nonzero direct IV effects. Together, these penalties help distinguish the spatial causal effect β⁡(𝐬)\beta(\mathbf{s}) from spatially heterogeneous IV effects αℓ​(𝐬)\alpha_{\ell}(\mathbf{s}).

The constraint requires that on every simplex at least one relevant instrument is treated as valid. The anchor constraint ties the two penalties together: it prevents the sparsity penalty from trading a few flagged blocks for an arbitrary shift of β\beta, because some instrument always remains unflagged and its ratio must be matched. Section A.2.2 of the Supplementary Material shows the requirements without a valid-IV plurality. Proposition A.2 in the Supplementary Material proves that there exists a unique minimizer with probability tending to 1. The Hi-FIVE estimators of β\beta and αℓ\alpha_{\ell} are:

β^(𝒔)=𝐁1(𝒔)⊤𝜽^β,α^ℓ(𝒔)=𝐁2(𝒔)⊤𝜽^α,ℓ,ℓ=1,…,p.\widehat{\beta}(\bm{s})=\mathbf{B}_{1}(\bm{s})^{\top}\widehat{\bm{\theta}}_{\beta},\qquad\widehat{\alpha}_{\ell}(\bm{s})=\mathbf{B}_{2}(\bm{s})^{\top}\widehat{\bm{\theta}}_{\alpha,\ell},\quad\ell=1,\ldots,p. (8)

2.3 Spatially Distributed Adaptive Learning

The optimization framework illustrated in Figure 2 provides an overview of the proposed spatially distributed adaptive learning procedure for Hi-FIVE. The local support of the spline basis enables parallel computation over spatial subdomains, substantially improving computational scalability for large-scale imaging data.

In addition, domain decomposition provides a flexible framework for modeling heterogeneous spatial effects over large and complex domains. The main motivation is that spatial smoothness, signal strength, and patterns of local IV validity may vary across different subdomains. By partitioning the full domain into several smaller subdomains, the proposed method can adaptively select subdomain-specific hyperparameters within each subdomain, rather than imposing a single set of global tuning parameters over the entire domain. This allows the Hi-FIVE estimators to better accommodate spatial heterogeneity while also reducing the computational burden for large-scale imaging data.

2.3.1 Distributed algorithm

We seek a minimizer of (6) by a distributed scheme that combines three ingredients: local linear approximation (LLA) of the nonconvex SCAD penalty, an alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) that enforces the smoothness constraint 𝚽1​𝜽β=𝟎\mathbf{\Phi}_{1}\bm{\theta}_{\beta}=\mathbf{0} across worker boundaries, and coordinate descent with group soft-thresholding for the region-wise invalid-IV blocks. Because the Bernstein–Bézier bases are locally supported, each update below is assembled from simplexwise contributions and parallelizes across workers.

2.3.2 Triangulation and tuning-parameter selection

In practice, we recommend using a finer triangulation to estimate the instrumental effects αℓ\alpha_{\ell} than for the causal effect β\beta. A finer triangulation resolves the boundary of an invalid region more sharply, thereby offering greater flexibility in identifying spatially varying invalid instruments. We employ a hierarchical triangulation scheme to facilitate distributed computation. Starting from an initial triangulation △1\triangle_{1}, we generate a refined triangulation △2\triangle_{2} through LL levels of uniform refinement, with each level subdividing every simplex into 2κ2^{\kappa} smaller ones. Throughout we take LL fixed, so that |△1||\triangle_{1}| and |△2||\triangle_{2}| are of the same order and K2=2κ​L​K1K_{2}=2^{\kappa L}K_{1}; unless stated otherwise we use L=1L=1. Figure 2 illustrates an example of △1\triangle_{1} and △2\triangle_{2}, with the green region highlighting a simplex assigned to a single worker and the orange regions representing the refined simplices within each worker.

For tuning parameter selection, we use a nested procedure. First, we fix a candidate value of the roughness penalty parameter λR\lambda^{\rm R}. Conditional on this value, we select the λS\lambda^{\rm S} by minimizing the modified BIC (mBIC). We then repeat this procedure over a grid of candidate values for λR\lambda^{\rm R} and choose the λR\lambda^{\rm R} using KK-fold cross-validation with folds formed at the subject level, so that within-image dependence is preserved.

We now introduce the mBIC criterion used to select λS\lambda^{\rm S}. Let 𝒜^λS={(ℓ,k):‖α^ℓ‖Tk≠0}\widehat{\mathcal{A}}_{\lambda^{S}}=\{(\ell,k):\|\widehat{\alpha}_{\ell}\|_{T_{k}}\neq 0\} be the estimated active set of invalid-IV blocks, among the p​K2pK_{2} candidate blocks. Write pISEλS=ISEλS+λRn​N​𝜽^β⊤​𝐏1​𝜽^β,\operatorname{pISE}_{\lambda^{S}}=\operatorname{ISE}_{\lambda^{S}}+\frac{\lambda^{R}}{nN}\widehat{\bm{\theta}}_{\beta}^{\top}\mathbf{P}_{1}\widehat{\bm{\theta}}_{\beta}, where ISEλS=1n​N​∑i=1n∑j=1N{Yi​(𝒔j)−(𝜸^⊤​𝐙i)​𝐁1⊤​(𝒔j)​𝜽^β−∑ℓ=1pZi​ℓ​𝐁2⊤​(𝒔j)​𝜽^α,ℓ}2.\text{ISE}_{\lambda^{S}}=\frac{1}{nN}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\Bigl\{Y_{i}(\bm{s}_{j})-(\widehat{\bm{\gamma}}^{\top}\mathbf{Z}_{i})\mathbf{B}_{1}^{\top}(\bm{s}_{j})\bm{\widehat{\theta}}_{\beta}-\sum_{\ell=1}^{p}Z_{i\ell}\mathbf{B}_{2}^{\top}(\bm{s}_{j})\bm{\widehat{\theta}}_{\alpha,\ell}\Bigr\}^{2}. To account for spatial dependence within simplices, consider the total effective sample size q^n=n​∑k=1K2N^eff,k,\widehat{q}_{n}=n\sum_{k=1}^{K_{2}}\widehat{N}_{\mathrm{eff},k}, where N^eff,k\widehat{N}_{\mathrm{eff},k} is the effective number of independent spatial observations within TkT_{k}; see Section A.2.5 for estimation details. When the pixels are nearly independent, q^n\widehat{q}_{n} is close to n​NnN; under strong spatial correlation, it is of order n​K2nK_{2}.

The mBIC is defined as:

mBIC⁡(λS)=log⁡(pISEλS)+|𝒜^λS|q^n​{log⁡q^n+2​a0​log⁡(p​K2)},a0∈(0,1),\operatorname{mBIC}(\lambda^{S})=\log\bigl(\operatorname{pISE}_{\lambda^{S}}\bigr)+\frac{|\widehat{\mathcal{A}}_{\lambda^{S}}|}{\widehat{q}_{n}}\bigl\{\log\widehat{q}_{n}+2a_{0}\log(pK_{2})\bigr\},\qquad a_{0}\in(0,1),

and λ^S\widehat{\lambda}^{\rm S} minimizes this criterion over a finite deterministic grid. The first term measures fit and roughness; the second penalizes the number of active invalid-IV blocks. The additional term 2​a0​log⁡(p​K2)2a_{0}\log(pK_{2}) accounts for the number of candidate supports (Chen and Chen, 2008). Section A.2.5 of the Supplementary Material investigates the theoretical properties of the proposed mBIC. Propositions A.3 and A.4 in the Supplementary Material show that the same oracle equality holds with probability tending to one when λS\lambda^{\rm S} is selected by mBIC over a finite grid, each under its own additional conditions.

3 Asymptotics and Simultaneous Inference

3.1 Properties of the Hi-FIVE Estimator

We next establish the asymptotic properties of Hi-FIVE. Our primary inferential target is the spatially varying causal effect β∗​(⋅)\beta^{\ast}(\cdot), while the regionwise invalid-IV effects αℓ​(⋅)\alpha_{\ell}(\cdot) are treated as nuisance components that capture local violations of the instrumental variable assumptions. Unlike classical variable-selection settings (Li et al., 2021), which typically assume sparsity among a large number of candidate variables, our domain-selection framework does not impose a sparsity assumption on the spatial regions affected by invalid IVs. Consequently, the invalid-IV effects are allowed to occupy nonvanishing portions of the spatial domain as the sample size increases. Moreover, observations within each region may be spatially correlated. Our analysis accommodates this dependence through the error covariance structure and region-specific effective sample sizes. For the asymptotic results below, we use the shorthand △≡△1\triangle\equiv\triangle_{1}. With fixed LL, we have |△2|≍|△||\triangle_{2}|\asymp|\triangle| and K2≍|△|−κK_{2}\asymp|\triangle|^{-\kappa}.

In the following, we partition the coefficient vector of (6) as 𝜽=(𝜽1⊤,𝜽2⊤)⊤\bm{\theta}=(\bm{\theta}_{1}^{\top},\bm{\theta}_{2}^{\top})^{\top}, where 𝜽1=(𝜽β⊤,{𝜽α,ℓ,k⊤:(ℓ,k)∈𝒜∗})⊤\bm{\theta}_{1}=(\bm{\theta}_{\beta}^{\top},\{\bm{\theta}_{\alpha,\ell,k}^{\top}:(\ell,k)\in\mathcal{A}^{\ast}\})^{\top} collects the causal-effect coefficients together with the coefficients of the truly invalid IV–simplex blocks, 𝒜∗={(ℓ,k):‖αℓ∗‖Tk>0}\mathcal{A}^{\ast}=\{(\ell,k):\|\alpha^{\ast}_{\ell}\|_{T_{k}}>0\}, and 𝜽2={𝜽α,ℓ,k:(ℓ,k)∉𝒜∗}\bm{\theta}_{2}=\{\bm{\theta}_{\alpha,\ell,k}:(\ell,k)\notin\mathcal{A}^{\ast}\} collects the remaining blocks, so that the true value satisfies 𝜽2∗=𝟎\bm{\theta}^{\ast}_{2}=\mathbf{0}. We define the oracle estimator 𝜽^1o\widehat{\bm{\theta}}^{\,o}_{1} as the minimizer of (6) over 𝜽1\bm{\theta}_{1} subject to 𝜽2=𝟎\bm{\theta}_{2}=\mathbf{0} and omitting the SCAD penalty, with the corresponding oracle estimator given by β^o​(⋅)=𝐁1​(⋅)⊤​𝜽^βo\widehat{\beta}^{\,o}(\cdot)=\mathbf{B}_{1}(\cdot)^{\top}\widehat{\bm{\theta}}^{\,o}_{\beta}.

Proposition A.2 in the Supplementary Material shows that, with probability tending to one, the oracle estimator is the unique global minimizer of the nonconvex criterion (6) under the anchor constraint (7). Consequently, the convergence rate (Theorem 2) and the pointwise asymptotic normality (Theorem 3) carry over from the oracle estimator to Hi-FIVE.

Theorem 2.

Under Assumptions B1–B8 in the Supplementary Material, with probability tending to one, criterion (6) under the anchor constraint (7) has a unique global minimizer 𝛉^=(𝛉^1⊤,𝛉^2⊤)⊤\widehat{\bm{\theta}}=(\widehat{\bm{\theta}}_{1}^{\top},\widehat{\bm{\theta}}_{2}^{\top})^{\top}. This minimizer has the following properties: (a) (Recovery of zero blocks) 𝛉^2=𝟎\widehat{\bm{\theta}}_{2}=\mathbf{0}; (b) (Oracle Equivalence) 𝛉^1=𝛉^1o\widehat{\bm{\theta}}_{1}=\widehat{\bm{\theta}}_{1}^{\,o}, so that the resulting Hi-FIVE estimator satisfies β^​(⋅)=β^o​(⋅)\widehat{\beta}(\cdot)=\widehat{\beta}^{\,o}(\cdot). Furthermore, the estimator β^\widehat{\beta} is L2L^{2}-consistent with convergence rate

‖β^−β∗‖L2​(Ω)=OP​{(1+λRn​N​|△|4)​|△|d+1​‖β∗‖d+1,∞+1n+λRn​N​|△|2​‖β∗‖2,∞}.\|\widehat{\beta}-\beta^{\ast}\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}=O_{\mathrm{P}}\left\{\left(1+\frac{\lambda^{\text{R}}}{nN|\triangle|^{4}}\right)|\triangle|^{d+1}\|\beta^{\ast}\|_{d+1,\infty}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}+\frac{\lambda^{\text{R}}}{nN|\triangle|^{2}}\|\beta^{\ast}\|_{2,\infty}\right\}.

The convergence rate in Theorem 2 explicitly captures the trade-off between the triangulation resolution |△||\triangle|, sample size nn, and spatial resolution NN. A finer partition (|△|→0|\triangle|\to 0) reduces spline approximation bias but increases the effective parameter dimension, requiring nn and NN to grow at compatible rates to maintain variance control.

Theorem 3.

σβ−1​(𝒔)​{β^​(𝒔)−β∗​(𝒔)}​⟶ℒ​N​(0,1),\sigma_{\beta}^{-1}(\bm{s})\left\{\widehat{\beta}(\bm{s})-\beta^{\ast}(\bm{s})\right\}\overset{\mathcal{L}}{\longrightarrow}N\left(0,1\right),

as n→∞n\to\infty, where σβ2​(𝐬)\sigma_{\beta}^{2}(\bm{s}) is the conditional oracle asymptotic variance defined in (A.23) of the Supplementary Material. Consequently, for 0<τ<10<\tau<1 and this fixed 𝐬\bm{s},

We replace them, respectively, by the fitted exposure D^i\widehat{D}_{i}, the support 𝒜^\widehat{\mathcal{A}} selected by Hi-FIVE, and the empirical covariance of the Hi-FIVE residuals Yi​(𝒔j)−Di​β^​(𝒔j)−𝐙i⊤​𝜶^​(𝒔j)Y_{i}(\bm{s}_{j})-D_{i}\widehat{\beta}(\bm{s}_{j})-\mathbf{Z}_{i}^{\top}\widehat{\bm{\alpha}}(\bm{s}_{j}). This gives the plug-in covariance 𝚵^\widehat{\bm{\Xi}} in (B.3) and hence σ^β2​(𝒔)\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{\beta}(\bm{s}) in (B.4); Supplementary Section B.2 gives the complete procedure, including the smoothed subject-level residual processes η^i​(⋅)\widehat{\eta}_{i}(\cdot) and the measurement-error residuals ε^i​j\widehat{\varepsilon}_{ij} used in the bootstrap below. Remark 1.

Since the fitted exposure is a linear combination of the candidate instruments, D^i=𝜸^⊤​𝐙i=∑ℓ=1pγ^ℓ​Zi​ℓ\widehat{D}_{i}=\widehat{\bm{\gamma}}^{\top}\mathbf{Z}_{i}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{p}\widehat{\gamma}_{\ell}Z_{i\ell}, the least-squares term in (5) depends on (β,{αℓ})(\beta,\{\alpha_{\ell}\}) only through the pp combined effect functions Γℓ​(𝒔)=γ^ℓ​β​(𝒔)+αℓ​(𝒔)\Gamma_{\ell}(\bm{s})=\widehat{\gamma}_{\ell}\,\beta(\bm{s})+\alpha_{\ell}(\bm{s}), ℓ=1,…,p\ell=1,\ldots,p, because D^i​β​(𝒔)+∑ℓZi​ℓ​αℓ​(𝒔)=∑ℓZi​ℓ​Γℓ​(𝒔)\widehat{D}_{i}\,\beta(\bm{s})+\sum_{\ell}Z_{i\ell}\alpha_{\ell}(\bm{s})=\sum_{\ell}Z_{i\ell}\Gamma_{\ell}(\bm{s}). Hence, for any shift function c⁡(⋅)c(\cdot), the reparametrization

(β,α1,…,αp)⟼(β−c,α1+γ^1​c,…,αp+γ^p​c)(\beta,\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{p})\longmapsto\bigl(\beta-c,\ \alpha_{1}+\widehat{\gamma}_{1}c,\ \ldots,\ \alpha_{p}+\widehat{\gamma}_{p}c\bigr) (14)

leaves the entire least-squares term unchanged. In such case, the fit alone does not identify β\beta: (14) is the finite-sample counterpart of the population non-identifiability that the plurality condition resolves (Definition 1 and Theorem 1). What separates the true representation from a shifted one is therefore not the fit but the penalties and the anchor constraint: a shift c≢0c\not\equiv 0 changes which invalid-IV blocks are nonzero, and hence the SCAD penalty, and the anchor constraint forbids any simplex on which every instrument is flagged. Theorems 2 and 3 formalize this through a joint separation condition Assumption B8(i): every incorrect anchored support with no more invalid-IV blocks than 𝒜∗\mathcal{A}^{\ast} must fit the reduced form worse, by a margin ΔnG\Delta_{n}^{\rm G} per block saved. When pointwise plurality holds everywhere, this condition is verified in Example A.1 of the Supplementary Material. Section A.2.2 of the Supplementary Material also shows that Hi-FIVE applies to regions where plurality fails: the anchor constraint (7) makes the condition hold there as well.

3.2 Bootstrap-calibrated Simultaneous Confidence Regions

Now, we use a wild bootstrap approach (Hall and Horowitz, 2013) to recalibrate pointwise confidence intervals (PCIs) and construct simultaneous confidence regions (SCRs). Given point estimates β^​(⋅)\widehat{\beta}(\cdot) and σ^β​(⋅)\widehat{\sigma}_{\beta}(\cdot), and nominal level τ0\tau_{0}, the procedure is described as follows:

  1. 1.

    Bootstrap Estimates. For b=1,…,Bb=1,\ldots,B, generate bootstrap samples {Yi∗(b)​(𝒔j),Di∗(b),𝐙i}\{Y^{*(b)}_{i}(\bm{s}_{j}),D_{i}^{*(b)},\mathbf{Z}_{i}\}, i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n, j=1,…,Nj=1,\ldots,N, using Yi∗(b)​(𝒔j)=Di∗(b)​β^​(𝒔j)+𝐙i⊤​𝜶^​(𝒔j)+νi(b)​η^i​(𝒔j)+νi​j(b)​ε^i​j,Di∗(b)=𝜸^⊤​𝐙i+νi(b)​ξ^i,Y_{i}^{\ast(b)}(\bm{s}_{j})=D_{i}^{\ast(b)}\widehat{\beta}(\bm{s}_{j})+\mathbf{Z}_{i}^{\top}\widehat{\bm{\alpha}}(\bm{s}_{j})+\nu_{i}^{(b)}\widehat{\eta}_{i}(\bm{s}_{j})+\nu_{ij}^{(b)}\widehat{\varepsilon}_{ij},D_{i}^{\ast(b)}=\widehat{\bm{\gamma}}^{\top}\mathbf{Z}_{i}+\nu_{i}^{(b)}\widehat{\xi}_{i}, where νi(b)\nu_{i}^{(b)} and νi​j(b)\nu_{ij}^{(b)} are independent Rademacher variables (taking values ±1\pm 1 with probability 0.5 each) and ξ^i=Di−𝜸^⊤​𝐙i\widehat{\xi}_{i}=D_{i}-\widehat{\bm{\gamma}}^{\top}\mathbf{Z}_{i}. Accordingly, compute β^∗(b)​(⋅)\widehat{\beta}^{*(b)}(\cdot) from (6) under (7) and σ^β∗(b)​(⋅)\widehat{\sigma}_{\beta}^{\ast(b)}(\cdot) from (B.4).

  2. 2.

    Recalibration. Solve the equation ι^​(τ)=1−τ0\widehat{\iota}(\tau)=1-\tau_{0} for τ\tau, and denote the root by τ^:=ι^−1​(1−τ0)\widehat{\tau}:=\widehat{\iota}^{-1}(1-\tau_{0}), where ι^​(τ)=B−1​∑b=1B𝕀⁡{β^​(𝒔j)∈[β^∗(b)​(𝒔j)±σ^β∗(b)​(𝒔j)​z1−τ/2],j=1,…,N}\widehat{\iota}(\tau)=B^{-1}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\mathbb{I}\big\{\widehat{\beta}(\bm{s}_{j})\in\big[\widehat{\beta}^{*(b)}(\bm{s}_{j})\pm\widehat{\sigma}_{\beta}^{*(b)}(\bm{s}_{j})z_{1-\tau/2}\big],j=1,\ldots,N\big\}. We construct SCR^​(𝒔)=[β^​(𝒔)±σ^β​(𝒔)​z1−τ^/2]\widehat{\rm SCR}(\bm{s})=\big[\widehat{\beta}(\bm{s})\pm\widehat{\sigma}_{\beta}(\bm{s})z_{1-\widehat{\tau}/2}\big].

The same multiplier νi(b)\nu_{i}^{(b)} is applied to both η^i\widehat{\eta}_{i} and ξ^i\widehat{\xi}_{i} so that the bootstrap preserves the dependence between the subject-level image process and the exposure error. Theorem 3 and Corollary B.1 in the supplementary materials provide theoretical justification for the pointwise intervals. The recalibration step is a finite-sample adjustment whose simultaneous coverage is assessed through simulation in Section 4.

4 Simulation Studies

We evaluate the estimation, simultaneous inference, robustness, and computational performance of Hi-FIVE through simulations. Because no existing functional-data method allows spatially varying invalid instruments, we compare Hi-FIVE with pointwise sisVIVE applied at each image location and with sisVIVE+ which smooths the pointwise sisVIVE estimates.

Simulation Design

For subject i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n and spatial location 𝒔j∈Ω\bm{s}_{j}\in\Omega, we generate

Yi​(𝒔j)\displaystyle Y_{i}(\bm{s}_{j}) =Di​β∗​(𝒔j)+𝐙i⊤​𝜶∗​(𝒔j)+ηi​(𝒔j)+εi​(𝒔j),Di=𝐙i⊤​𝜸∗+ξi,\displaystyle=D_{i}\beta^{\ast}(\bm{s}_{j})+\mathbf{Z}_{i}^{\top}\bm{\alpha}^{\ast}(\bm{s}_{j})+\eta_{i}(\bm{s}_{j})+\varepsilon_{i}(\bm{s}_{j}),\quad D_{i}=\mathbf{Z}_{i}^{\top}\bm{\gamma}^{\ast}+\xi_{i},

where β∗​(⋅)\beta^{\ast}(\cdot) is the causal-effect function and 𝜶∗​(⋅)\bm{\alpha}^{\ast}(\cdot) is the spatially varying invalid-IV effect. The spatial process ηi​(⋅)\eta_{i}(\cdot) is correlated with ξi\xi_{i} to induce unmeasured confounding. We consider n∈{100,300}n\in\{100,300\}, p∈{3,10}p\in\{3,10\}, and low- and high-noise settings. The two-dimensional (2D) images contain 95×7995\times 79 pixels, and the three-dimensional (3D) images contain 67367^{3} voxels.

The invalid-IV configuration is constructed to violate pointwise plurality. Let q=⌊p/2⌋+1q=\lfloor p/2\rfloor+1. The first qq instruments share a common nonzero invalid-IV effect over a localized region ℛα\mathcal{R}_{\alpha}, while the remaining instruments are valid throughout the domain. Hence, the invalid instruments form the largest ratio group within ℛα\mathcal{R}_{\alpha}, although the spatial identifiability conditions in Section 2.1 continue to hold.

We consider three scenarios: a smooth 2D causal effect, a 2D causal effect with a jump discontinuity, and a smooth 3D causal effect. The exact coefficient functions, invalid-IV regions ℛα\mathcal{R}_{\alpha}, covariance parameters, signal-to-noise ratios (SNR), triangulations, and tuning specifications are provided in Sections C.1–C.2 in the Supplementary Material. Specifically, the first-stage SNR, defined in Equation (C.1) as a measure of the candidate IV strength, ranges from approximately 0.2 to 0.4. The second-stage SNR, which measures the strength of the imaging outcome signal, ranges from 1 to 2 under the high-noise setting and from 4 to 8 under the low-noise setting. For each configuration, we generate 200 Monte Carlo replications and report the mean integrated squared error MISE=R−1​∑r=1RISE(r){\rm MISE}=R^{-1}\sum^{R}_{r=1}\text{ISE}^{(r)} and SDISE={(R−1)−1​∑r=1R{ISE(r)−MISE}2}1/2\text{SD}_{\text{ISE}}=\{(R-1)^{-1}\sum^{R}_{r=1}\{\text{ISE}^{(r)}-\text{MISE}\}^{2}\}^{1/2}, where ISE(r)=N−1​∑j=1N{β∗​(𝒔j)−β^(r)​(𝒔j)}2\text{ISE}^{(r)}=N^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\{\beta^{\ast}(\bm{s}_{j})-\widehat{\beta}^{(r)}(\bm{s}_{j})\}^{2}. Simultaneous inference is assessed using the Empirical Coverage Rates ECR=R−1∑r=1RI{β∗(𝒔j)∈SCR^1−τ(r)(𝒔j) for all j}\text{ECR}=R^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^{R}I\{\beta^{\ast}(\bm{s}_{j})\in\widehat{\rm SCR}^{(r)}_{1-\tau}(\bm{s}_{j})\text{ for all }j\} and average confidence region widths.

Causal-Effect Estimation

Figure 3 summarizes the estimation results across all settings. Tables C.4–C.6 in the Supplementary Material report the corresponding numerical values. Under the common-ratio invalid group used here, pointwise plurality fails on ℛα\mathcal{R}_{\alpha}. In the two-dimensional (2D) settings, Hi-FIVE attains the smallest MISE in every configuration, with particularly large improvements where the pointwise plurality condition fails. Increasing the sample size reduces both the estimation error and Monte Carlo variability of Hi-FIVE. In contrast, sisVIVE remains substantially biased because it performs identification independently at each location. Although sisVIVE+ reduces local variability through post-smoothing, it cannot remove the bias caused by failed pointwise identification.

Figure 4(a) shows representative estimated surfaces in the smooth 2D setting. Hi-FIVE closely recovers the true causal effect. In contrast, the sisVIVE estimate is noisy, and its error is dominated by bias in the invalid-IV regions. Smoothing in sisVIVE+ removes much of the noise, but this bias remains clearly visible.

We next consider a causal-effect function with a jump discontinuity. This design violates the continuity assumption of Theorem 1 and the smoothness assumption of Theorems 2–3, so it is a misspecification study rather than a setting covered by the theory; in particular, a jump of β∗\beta^{\ast} across a region boundary is not distinguishable from an invalid-IV effect by the identification argument alone. The true signal forms a digital-font “4,” while the invalid-IV effect occupies the additional region required to form an “H.” Thus, a method that fails to separate the causal and invalid-IV effects tends to recover an H-shaped coefficient function. As shown in Figure 3, under low noise, the Hi-FIVE estimator improves clearly as the sample size increases, with substantial decreases in both the MISE and its standard deviation. Under high noise, Hi-FIVE still achieves the lowest MISE across all nonsmooth settings. Figure 4(b) shows that the comparison methods tend to mix the invalid-IV signal with the true causal effect and estimate an H-shaped jump in the causal-effect function. In contrast, the Hi-FIVE estimator mostly preserves the “4” pattern, suggesting that it can distinguish the causal-effect structure from the invalid-IV pattern. Although Hi-FIVE is designed for a continuous causal-effect function and therefore does not perfectly recover the discontinuity, it still captures the main causal pattern and remains robust in nonsmooth settings. Its MISE in this design is, however, an order of magnitude larger than in the smooth design (Tables C.4 and C.5), which quantifies the cost of the misspecification.

We further evaluate Hi-FIVE for three-dimensional (3D) volumetric outcomes. Figure C.4 displays estimates from Hi-FIVE and the comparison methods for selected 3D slices. This setting is more challenging because of the substantially larger number of spatial locations, the increased computational burden, and the more complex geometry of spatially localized invalid-IV effects. Nevertheless, Hi-FIVE consistently attains the smallest MISE across all configurations. Its advantage becomes more pronounced as the sample size increases, accompanied by a substantial reduction in the standard deviation of the MISE and a wider performance gap relative to sisVIVE+. These results show that the proposed spatial identification and estimation framework performs effectively in 3D settings.

Inferences and Computational Cost

Table 1 evaluates the inference performance of Hi-FIVE in the 2D smooth case at significance level τ∈{0.1,0.05,0.01}\tau\in\{0.1,0.05,0.01\}. Across most settings, empirical coverage rates are close to their nominal levels 1−τ1-\tau. As expected, the SCR widths increase when the nominal level becomes lower, from τ=0.10\tau=0.10 to τ=0.01\tau=0.01, and they are generally wider under high noise. Increasing the sample size from n=100n=100 to n=300n=300 reduces the SCR widths, reflecting improved estimation precision. In addition, the SCRs are also narrower for p=10p=10 than for p=3p=3, suggesting that the additional IV information improves the inference efficiency.

Table 2 reports the average computational time for model estimation on a standard computing platform. Hi-FIVE is substantially faster than sisVIVE, particularly in the 3D setting, while its computational time increases moderately with sample size, number of instruments, and image dimension. Moreover, we assess triangulation sensitivity by considering coarse, default, and fine triangulations; see Section C.6 in the Supplementary Material. The estimated causal effects and invalid-IV regions remain stable, while finer triangulations improve boundary resolution at additional computational cost.

5 Application

Hi-FIVE is applied to data from the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI). The imaging responses are spatially normalized fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) images of size 79×\times95×\times68, which measure regional glucose metabolism, a widely used proxy for neuronal activity. We consider phosphorylated tau (p-tau) as the exposure, and five SNPs (rs744373, rs3820757, rs11136000, rs6656401, rs3851179), chosen from prior genetic and biomarker studies of tau pathology and CSF AD biomarkers (Franzmeier et al., 2019; Franzmeier et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2020), as candidate instrumental variables. Age, sex, and diagnosis are partialled out of the imaging outcome, exposure, and instruments before the two-stage fit. The complete-case sample with baseline FDG-PET, p-tau, genotype, and covariates comprises 105 subjects: 29 cognitively normal, 39 early MCI, and 37 MCI participants; none had dementia, because the matched genotype–imaging subset was concentrated among cognitively normal and MCI participants. We have no evidence that any of these SNPs violates the IV assumptions, but their pointwise validity cannot be guaranteed since their biological functions and potential pleiotropic pathways are not fully understood, a common issue in MR. Because some SNPs are involved in the broader pathway linking Aβ\beta, p-tau, and cognition, they may affect FDG-PET through mechanisms other than p-tau, which motivates our analysis allowing for invalid IVs. As a key biomarker of tau-related AD pathology closely associated with downstream neurodegeneration, p-tau lets us assess whether tau burden causally affects neurodegeneration, as reflected by FDG-PET across brain regions. To accommodate potential differences in spatial effects between hemispheres, we partition the image domain into left- and right-hemisphere subdomains.

Figure 5 (A1)-(A3) shows the estimated causal effects of p-tau on FDG-PET metabolism. Blue regions represent negative causal effects, suggesting that higher p-tau leads to reduced metabolic activity under the fitted IV model, whereas red regions indicate positive causal effects, and green regions correspond to estimates close to zero. In the 3D causal-effect maps, s1s_{1}, s2s_{2}, and s3s_{3} denote sagittal, coronal, and axial slice indices, respectively.

Across these views, the estimated causal effect of p-tau on FDG-PET is negative in localized regions, most prominently in the left-hemispheric sagittal slice (s1=60s_{1}=60), posterior coronal slices (s2=25s_{2}=25 and s2=40s_{2}=40), and mid-to-superior axial slices (s3=36s_{3}=36 and s3=45s_{3}=45). Under the fitted model, these negative patterns indicate that higher p-tau lowers FDG-PET uptake there. Their spatial distribution is consistent with previous ADNI studies linking elevated plasma or CSF pTau181 to lower FDG metabolism in cognitively impaired individuals, particularly in temporal, cingulate, precuneus, and orbitofrontal regions (Shen et al., 2021). The axial slices also cover posterior cingulate, precuneus, and parietotemporal regions, which are commonly hypometabolic on FDG-PET in MCI and AD (Bailly et al., 2015). Although these prior findings are associational, they support the biological plausibility of our causal estimates. Some positive estimates are observed, particularly in the near-midline sagittal slice (s1=40s_{1}=40). Because prior evidence most consistently links p-tau to reduced glucose metabolism, we interpret these positive regions as localized effects in this nondemented cohort rather than as a typical AD-related pattern.

The 3D significance map in Figure 5 (B1)-(B2) further indicates significant heterogeneous Hi-FIVE causal effects of p-tau on FDG-PET, with significant positive clusters primarily in anterior regions and significant negative clusters in posterior and inferior regions. The posterior negative pattern is consistent with AD-related FDG-PET hypometabolism in the posterior cingulate, precuneus, and temporoparietal cortex (Wilson et al., 2019; Hanseeuw et al., 2017). The anterior positive clusters may reflect localized metabolic increases that differ from the typical posterior hypometabolic pattern, consistent with prior evidence linking p-tau181 to FDG-PET abnormalities and reports of tau-related FDG-PET hypermetabolism in the MCI group (Shen et al., 2021; Rubinski et al., 2020).

6 Discussion

We propose Hi-FIVE, a functional data approach for causal estimation with imaging outcomes under unmeasured confounding. Hi-FIVE leverages spatial structure to relax the plurality requirement for valid IVs, enabling identification and inference in settings where scalar-outcome methods fail. It also uses domain decomposition and local basis representations to improve computational scalability while preserving localized spatial features. Simulations show that Hi-FIVE achieves lower estimation error and more accurate invalid-IV selection than pixelwise competitors and their smoothed variants.

The framework suggests several extensions. First, the current theory treats the number of candidate IVs as fixed; accommodating a very large instrument set is an important open problem. Second, weak instruments remain a serious obstacle in genetic applications, and how instrument strength interacts with the relaxed plurality condition is not yet understood (Lin et al., 2024; Ye et al., 2024). Third, we have assumed throughout that the causal effect function is continuous; adapting both the estimator and the theory to effects that jump across anatomical boundaries is an open problem. Fourth, many genome-wide studies release only summary statistics computed on separate exposure and outcome samples, and a two-sample version of Hi-FIVE would widen its applicability considerably (Ye et al., 2021; Dai et al., 2024; Zilinskas et al., 2024). Finally, the identification argument is not specific to IVs and may prove useful for other functional causal estimands, particularly mediation analysis with imaging mediators.

rℓ​(𝒔)=β⁡(𝒔)+αℓ​(𝒔)γℓ∗=β~​(𝒔)+α~ℓ​(𝒔)γℓ∗,𝒔∈Ω.r_{\ell}(\bm{s})=\beta(\bm{s})+\frac{\alpha_{\ell}(\bm{s})}{\gamma^{\ast}_{\ell}}=\widetilde{\beta}(\bm{s})+\frac{\widetilde{\alpha}_{\ell}(\bm{s})}{\gamma^{\ast}_{\ell}},\qquad\bm{s}\in\Omega. (A.2)

Step 1: Existence of a coincidence point.

We first show that the two causal effect functions coincide at some point of Ω\Omega. Since the ratio surfaces rℓ​(⋅)r_{\ell}(\cdot), ℓ∈ℐ\ell\in\mathcal{I}, are determined by the observed distribution, condition (A2)(b) is not pair-specific: either it holds for both observationally equivalent parameter pairs, or it holds for neither. In the latter case, since each pair satisfies (A2), both pairs must satisfy (A2)(a).

Suppose that (A2)(b) holds. Then there exists a nonempty open set Ω⨀⊆Ω\Omega_{\bigodot}\subseteq\Omega such that rℓ​(𝒔)=rk​(𝒔)r_{\ell}(\bm{s})=r_{k}(\bm{s}) for all ℓ,k∈ℐ\ell,k\in\mathcal{I} and all 𝒔∈Ω⨀\bm{s}\in\Omega_{\bigodot}. Fix any 𝒔∈Ω⨀\bm{s}\in\Omega_{\bigodot}. By (A1), applied to (β,𝜶)(\beta,\bm{\alpha}), there exists at least one relevant IV ℓ∈ℐ\ell\in\mathcal{I} such that αℓ​(𝒔)=0\alpha_{\ell}(\bm{s})=0. Then (A.1) gives rℓ​(𝒔)=β​(𝒔)r_{\ell}(\bm{s})=\beta(\bm{s}). Since all ratio values are equal on Ω⨀\Omega_{\bigodot}, their common value equals β⁡(𝒔)\beta(\bm{s}). Similarly, by (A1), applied to (β~,𝜶~)(\widetilde{\beta},\widetilde{\bm{\alpha}}), there exists k∈ℐk\in\mathcal{I} such that α~k​(𝒔)=0\widetilde{\alpha}_{k}(\bm{s})=0, and hence rk​(𝒔)=β~​(𝒔)r_{k}(\bm{s})=\widetilde{\beta}(\bm{s}). Therefore β​(𝒔)=β~​(𝒔)\beta(\bm{s})=\widetilde{\beta}(\bm{s}), so U:=Ω⨀U:=\Omega_{\bigodot} is a nonempty open set on which the two causal effect functions coincide.

Suppose that (A2)(a) holds. There exist Lebesgue-measurable sets Ω⊕⊆Ω0​(β,𝜶)\Omega_{\oplus}\subseteq\Omega_{0}(\beta,\bm{\alpha}) and Ω~⊕⊆Ω0​(β~,𝜶~)\widetilde{\Omega}_{\oplus}\subseteq\Omega_{0}(\widetilde{\beta},\widetilde{\bm{\alpha}}) such that Vol⁡(Ω⊕)>Vol⁡(Ω)/2{\rm Vol}(\Omega_{\oplus})>{\rm Vol}(\Omega)/2 and Vol⁡(Ω~⊕)>Vol⁡(Ω)/2{\rm Vol}(\widetilde{\Omega}_{\oplus})>{\rm Vol}(\Omega)/2. |{ℓ∈ℐ:rℓ​(𝒔)=β⁡(𝒔)}|>maxv≠β⁡(𝒔)⁡|{ℓ∈ℐ:rℓ​(𝒔)=v}|,\left|\{\ell\in\mathcal{I}:r_{\ell}(\bm{s})=\beta(\bm{s})\}\right|>\max_{v\neq\beta(\bm{s})}\left|\{\ell\in\mathcal{I}:r_{\ell}(\bm{s})=v\}\right|,

Define S:={𝒔∈Ω:β⁡(𝒔)=β~​(𝒔)}S:=\{\bm{s}\in\Omega:\beta(\bm{s})=\widetilde{\beta}(\bm{s})\}. Since β,β~∈Cr​(Ω)\beta,\widetilde{\beta}\in C^{r}(\Omega), both functions are continuous, and therefore SS is closed in Ω\Omega. By Step 1, SS is nonempty. We show that S=ΩS=\Omega.

Step 3: Counterexamples when one assumption fails.

Take Ω=[0,1]2\Omega=[0,1]^{2}, a compact, connected domain with nonempty interior. The following two-dimensional examples show that failure of each condition can lead to non-identifiability. To construct the common observed distribution, take mean-zero ξ\xi and a mean-zero process u⁡(⋅)u(\cdot) with (ξ,u⁡(⋅))(\xi,u(\cdot)) independent of 𝐙\mathbf{Z}, and set D=𝐙⊤​𝜸+ξD=\mathbf{Z}^{\top}\bm{\gamma}+\xi and Y⁡(𝒔)=𝐙⊤​ϖ​(𝒔)+u⁡(𝒔)Y(\bm{s})=\mathbf{Z}^{\top}\bm{\varpi}(\bm{s})+u(\bm{s}). For each pair satisfying 𝜸​β+𝜶=ϖ\bm{\gamma}\beta+\bm{\alpha}=\bm{\varpi}, define ϵ⁡(𝒔)=u⁡(𝒔)−ξ​β​(𝒔)\epsilon(\bm{s})=u(\bm{s})-\xi\beta(\bm{s}). Then (3) and both orthogonality conditions hold, while the observed distribution is the same for every such pair. Dependence between ξ\xi and ϵ\epsilon is allowed in the identifiability theorem.

Failure of (A1): Let p=2p=2, 𝜸=(1,1)⊤\bm{\gamma}=(1,1)^{\top}, and let r1​(𝒔)=r2​(𝒔)=0r_{1}(\bm{s})=r_{2}(\bm{s})=0 for all 𝒔∈Ω\bm{s}\in\Omega. Consider Model A with βA​(𝒔)=0\beta_{A}(\bm{s})=0 and 𝜶A​(𝒔)=(0,0)⊤\bm{\alpha}_{A}(\bm{s})=(0,0)^{\top}, and Model B with βB​(𝒔)=1\beta_{B}(\bm{s})=1 and 𝜶B​(𝒔)=(−1,−1)⊤\bm{\alpha}_{B}(\bm{s})=(-1,-1)^{\top}. Then

𝜸​βA​(𝒔)+𝜶A​(𝒔)=(0,0)⊤=𝜸​βB​(𝒔)+𝜶B​(𝒔),\bm{\gamma}\beta_{A}(\bm{s})+\bm{\alpha}_{A}(\bm{s})=(0,0)^{\top}=\bm{\gamma}\beta_{B}(\bm{s})+\bm{\alpha}_{B}(\bm{s}),

so the two models are observationally equivalent, but βA​(𝒔)≠βB​(𝒔)\beta_{A}(\bm{s})\neq\beta_{B}(\bm{s}). In Model B, no relevant IV is valid anywhere, because both components of 𝜶B\bm{\alpha}_{B} are equal to −1-1. Hence (A1) fails. However, (A2)(b) holds because all ratio surfaces are equal on Ω\Omega, and (A3) holds because the components of 𝜶B\bm{\alpha}_{B} are constant and both IVs are invalid everywhere, hence stable everywhere. Therefore, without (A1), β⁡(⋅)\beta(\cdot) is generally not identifiable.

Failure of (A2): Let p=2p=2, 𝜸=(1,1)⊤\bm{\gamma}=(1,1)^{\top}, and let r1​(𝒔)=0r_{1}(\bm{s})=0 and r2​(𝒔)=1r_{2}(\bm{s})=1 for all 𝒔∈Ω\bm{s}\in\Omega. Consider Model A with βA​(𝒔)=0\beta_{A}(\bm{s})=0 and 𝜶A​(𝒔)=(0,1)⊤\bm{\alpha}_{A}(\bm{s})=(0,1)^{\top}, and Model B with βB​(𝒔)=1\beta_{B}(\bm{s})=1 and 𝜶B​(𝒔)=(−1,0)⊤\bm{\alpha}_{B}(\bm{s})=(-1,0)^{\top}. Then

𝜸​βA​(𝒔)+𝜶A​(𝒔)=(0,1)⊤=𝜸​βB​(𝒔)+𝜶B​(𝒔),\bm{\gamma}\beta_{A}(\bm{s})+\bm{\alpha}_{A}(\bm{s})=(0,1)^{\top}=\bm{\gamma}\beta_{B}(\bm{s})+\bm{\alpha}_{B}(\bm{s}),

so the two models are observationally equivalent, but βA​(𝒔)≡0\beta_{A}(\bm{s})\equiv 0 and βB​(𝒔)≡1\beta_{B}(\bm{s})\equiv 1. In Model A, Z1Z_{1} is valid everywhere and Z2Z_{2} is invalid everywhere, while in Model B, Z2Z_{2} is valid everywhere and Z1Z_{1} is invalid everywhere. Thus (A1) holds for both models. The components of 𝜶A\bm{\alpha}_{A} and 𝜶B\bm{\alpha}_{B} are constant, so every IV has a stable validity status, and (A3) holds. However, (A2) fails. At every 𝒔\bm{s}, the observable ratio multiset is {0,1}\{0,1\}, so there is no strict plurality value, and there is no nonempty open set on which all relevant ratio surfaces are equal. Therefore, without (A2), β⁡(⋅)\beta(\cdot) is generally not identifiable.

Failure of (A3): Let p=3p=3, 𝜸=(1,1,1)⊤\bm{\gamma}=(1,1,1)^{\top}, and define g⁡(𝒔)=(s1−2/3)+r+1g(\bm{s})=(s_{1}-2/3)_{+}^{r+1} for 𝒔=(s1,s2)∈[0,1]2\bm{s}=(s_{1},s_{2})\in[0,1]^{2}, where (x)+=max⁡(x,0)(x)_{+}=\max(x,0). Then

𝜸​βA​(𝒔)+𝜶A​(𝒔)=(0,0,g⁡(𝒔))⊤=𝜸​βB​(𝒔)+𝜶B​(𝒔),\bm{\gamma}\beta_{A}(\bm{s})+\bm{\alpha}_{A}(\bm{s})=(0,0,g(\bm{s}))^{\top}=\bm{\gamma}\beta_{B}(\bm{s})+\bm{\alpha}_{B}(\bm{s}),

so the two models are observationally equivalent, but βA​(𝒔)≡0\beta_{A}(\bm{s})\equiv 0 whereas βB​(𝒔)=g​(𝒔)\beta_{B}(\bm{s})=g(\bm{s}), and these differ on {s1>2/3}\{s_{1}>2/3\}. Assumption (A1) holds: in Model A, Z1Z_{1} and Z2Z_{2} are valid everywhere, while in Model B, Z3Z_{3} is valid everywhere. Assumption (A2) also holds, because on the nonempty open set Ω⨀:={𝒔∈[0,1]2:s1<2/3}\Omega_{\bigodot}:=\{\bm{s}\in[0,1]^{2}:s_{1}<2/3\}, r1=r2=r3=0r_{1}=r_{2}=r_{3}=0. However, (A3) fails. For Model B, when s1≤2/3s_{1}\leq 2/3, all three IVs are valid; when s1>2/3s_{1}>2/3, only Z3Z_{3} is valid. Hence the pointwise plurality region for Model B is Ω0​(βB,𝜶B)={𝒔∈Ω:s1≤2/3}\Omega_{0}(\beta_{B},\bm{\alpha}_{B})=\{\bm{s}\in\Omega:s_{1}\leq 2/3\}, so clΩ​{Ω0​(βB,𝜶B)c}={𝒔∈Ω:s1≥2/3}{\rm cl}_{\Omega}\{\Omega_{0}(\beta_{B},\bm{\alpha}_{B})^{c}\}=\{\bm{s}\in\Omega:s_{1}\geq 2/3\}. Take any boundary point 𝒕=(2/3,t2)\bm{t}=(2/3,t_{2}). Then 𝒕∈clΩ​{Ω0​(βB,𝜶B)c}\bm{t}\in{\rm cl}_{\Omega}\{\Omega_{0}(\beta_{B},\bm{\alpha}_{B})^{c}\}, and αB,1​(𝒔)=αB,2​(𝒔)=−g⁡(𝒔)\alpha_{B,1}(\bm{s})=\alpha_{B,2}(\bm{s})=-g(\bm{s}) are CrC^{r} in a neighborhood of 𝒕\bm{t}. However, Z1Z_{1} and Z2Z_{2} are valid on the side s1≤2/3s_{1}\leq 2/3 and invalid on the side s1>2/3s_{1}>2/3, so every neighborhood of 𝒕\bm{t} contains both valid and invalid points for these IVs. Thus Z1Z_{1} and Z2Z_{2} are unstable at 𝒕\bm{t}, contradicting (A3). Therefore, if (A3) is dropped, two different causal effect functions yield the same observed distribution, and β⁡(⋅)\beta(\cdot) is not identifiable.

Combining Steps 1 and 2 proves identifiability under (A1)–(A3), and the three examples in Step 3 show that failure of any one of these assumptions can generally lead to non-identifiability. ∎

Remarks on the assumptions.
Remark A.1 (Spline approximation and invalid instruments).

Assumptions B1, B2 and B7 are standard in spline estimation over triangulations; see Lai and Schumaker (2007) and Yu et al. (2021). Quasi-uniformity excludes degenerate simplices, while smoothness and the rate conditions control the approximation and roughness-penalty biases.

The fixed refinement level gives 𝒮dr​(△1)⊆𝒮d−1​(△2)\mathcal{S}_{d}^{r}(\triangle_{1})\subseteq\mathcal{S}_{d}^{-1}(\triangle_{2}) and comparable mesh sizes. The elementwise L2L^{2} projection error of each αℓ∗\alpha_{\ell}^{\ast} is orthogonal to the causal spline space in the population inner product. Lemma A.5 bounds its empirical contribution; population orthogonality does not make that contribution zero. Nesting also places all fitted spatial vectors in a common broken spline space, as used in Lemma A.10.

Assumption B3 allows validity to vary spatially but requires a relevant valid instrument at each location. Its lower bound on nonzero effects is a signal-size condition for support recovery (Fan and Li, 2001; Wainwright, 2009).

Remark A.2 (Error covariance and effective sample size).

Assumptions B4 and B6 provide independent subjects, exponential concentration and a well-conditioned population design (Vershynin, 2018; Wainwright, 2009). Within-subject spatial dependence is described by Assumption B5. Since ρϵ≤1\rho_{\epsilon}\leq 1, Neff,k≥1N_{\mathrm{eff},k}\geq 1; if correlations are nonnegative, then also Neff,k≤mkN_{\mathrm{eff},k}\leq m_{k}. Under nonnegative correlations, the effective sample size therefore ranges from one observation under perfect dependence to mkm_{k} under independence. Quasi-uniformity gives comparable pixel counts across simplices, while Neff−≥c0​N¯effN^{-}_{\mathrm{eff}}\geq c_{0}\bar{N}_{\mathrm{eff}} additionally requires comparable effective sample sizes. This condition permits the two effective sample sizes to be interchanged up to a constant.

The pilot condition Neff+​{log⁡N/n+ϱn}→0N^{+}_{\mathrm{eff}}\{\sqrt{\log N/n}+\varrho_{n}\}\to 0 is used in Lemma A.11 to estimate qnq_{n}. It is not used by Theorems 2 and 3 or Proposition A.2.

Remark A.3 (Global signal separation and selection).

Assumption B8 compares the joint causal and invalid-effect fit with every incorrect anchored support containing no more blocks than the true support. Both β\beta and the retained α\alpha blocks may change. The neighborhood of 𝜸∗\bm{\gamma}^{\ast} accommodates the estimated first stage. The first bound in (A.12) makes the cost of an additional block exceed the total stochastic gain in fit; the second prevents the savings from deleting blocks from exceeding their loss of fit. The first bound is sufficient and is not asserted to be sharp.

According to the Hi-FIVE criterion, the comparison family contains only anchored supports. This matters when pointwise plurality fails: the invariance (14) produces representations that reproduce the reduced form exactly and, when valid instruments are a minority on a region of fixed size, use fewer blocks than 𝒜∗\mathcal{A}^{\ast} once the mesh is fine; such representations must flag every instrument on a transition band and are therefore not anchored. Anchored supports keep an unflagged instrument on every simplex, so a transition band incurs a loss of fit. Section A.2.2 verifies part (i) in this regime with ΔnG≍bn2​|△|κ+1\Delta_{n}^{\rm G}\asymp b_{n}^{2}|\triangle|^{\kappa+1}, where bnb_{n} is the size of the invalid-IV effect.

Lemma A.13 uses this joint gap to compare incorrect supports of no larger size. Proposition A.3 excludes larger supports from the global SCAD path through (A.45). Proposition A.4 instead compares all anchored supports under its additional conditions.

Remark A.4 (Conditions for pointwise normality).

Assumption B9 is used by the oracle and Hi-FIVE pointwise limit laws and by Corollary B.1. It is not needed for the convergence rates or support recovery. Conditions (U1)–(U2) make the spline approximation and roughness biases o(n−1/2)o(n^{-1/2}) at the location under study. The available pointwise bounds lose a factor |△|−κ/2|\triangle|^{-\kappa/2} relative to the L2L^{2} bounds, so Assumption B7 alone does not imply (U1)–(U2). Condition (U3) makes the number of basis functions smaller in order than the number of subjects and gives the required Lindeberg bound.

Condition (V) separately requires a nondegenerate pointwise variance. The heuristic n​σβ2​(𝒔)≈Gη​(𝒔,𝒔)n\sigma_{\beta}^{2}(\bm{s})\approx G_{\eta}(\bm{s},\bm{s}) comes from spline reproduction of smooth functions, but is not proved here. In particular, the rate examples below do not verify (V). Sharper bounds on the inverse Gram matrix in the locally supported basis could reduce the undersmoothing requirements: the intended relaxations replace (U1) by the approximation rate in Assumption B7, replace (U2) by n1/2​λR​(n​N)−1→0n^{1/2}\lambda^{\rm R}(nN)^{-1}\to 0, and remove (U3). Such equivalent-kernel bounds are not established here and are not used in the stated results.

For |△|≍n−a|\triangle|\asymp n^{-a}, the rate restrictions in Assumptions B3 and B7, combined with Assumption B8 when ΔnG≍|△|κ​n−2​c\Delta_{n}^{\rm G}\asymp|\triangle|^{\kappa}n^{-2c} as in Example A.1 (so that n−1n^{-1} and |△|2​d+2|\triangle|^{2d+2}, both bounded by en,Ne_{n,N}, are o⁡(ΔnG)o(\Delta_{n}^{\rm G})), require

12​(d+1)<a<1−2​cκ,a⁡(d+1−κ/2)>c.\frac{1}{2(d+1)}<a<\frac{1-2c}{\kappa},\qquad a(d+1-\kappa/2)>c.

For suitable NN and λR\lambda^{\rm R}, these inequalities can hold if and only if κ<2​(d+1)\kappa<2(d+1) and c<1/2−κ/{4​(d+1)}c<1/2-\kappa/\{4(d+1)\}, explaining the upper bound in Assumption B3. Condition (U1) of Assumption B9 further requires

12​(d+1)−κ<a<1−2​cκ.\frac{1}{2(d+1)-\kappa}<a<\frac{1-2c}{\kappa}.

This interval is nonempty if and only if c<1/2−κ/{4​(d+1)−2​κ}c<1/2-\kappa/\{4(d+1)-2\kappa\}. These comparisons concern the rate conditions. Joint signal separation and the variance lower bound remain separate requirements.

A.2.2 Joint Separation under Anchoring when Plurality Fails

This section supports Remark 1 of the main paper. It verifies Assumption B8(i) for the Hi-FIVE criterion under the anchor constraint (7) in a mesh-aligned idealization of the simulation designs, with an invalid region of fixed size, which is the regime in which valid instruments may be a minority on a region of positive volume. The critical competitors are generated by the invariance (14): for g∈𝒮dr​(△1)g\in\mathcal{S}^{r}_{d}(\triangle_{1}), the representation (β∗+g,α1∗−γ1∗​g,…,αp∗−γp∗​g)(\beta^{\ast}+g,\ \alpha^{\ast}_{1}-\gamma^{\ast}_{1}g,\ldots,\alpha^{\ast}_{p}-\gamma^{\ast}_{p}g) has the same combined effects γℓ∗​β+αℓ\gamma^{\ast}_{\ell}\beta+\alpha_{\ell} as (β∗,𝜶∗)(\beta^{\ast},\bm{\alpha}^{\ast}) and reproduces the population reduced form exactly, so it can be ruled out only through the block count and the anchor constraint. Throughout, blocks are counted at the population first stage 𝜸∗\bm{\gamma}^{\ast}. Figure A.1 illustrates the mechanism in a one-dimensional cross-section. On every simplex, anchoring leaves some instrument unflagged and thereby ties the fitted causal effect to that instrument’s ratio rℓ=β∗+αℓ∗/γℓ∗r_{\ell}=\beta^{\ast}+\alpha^{\ast}_{\ell}/\gamma^{\ast}_{\ell}; the two lemmas below quantify the loss of fit this forces on a competitor that exchanges the valid and invalid groups on part of ℛα\mathcal{R}_{\alpha}, and Proposition A.1 compares that loss with the number of blocks saved.

Setting.

Let Ω\Omega be a bounded polyhedral Lipschitz domain with connected interior and Vol⁡(Ω)=1\operatorname{Vol}(\Omega)=1. Let △(0)\triangle^{(0)} be a fixed triangulation of Ω\Omega, and let each △1\triangle_{1} be obtained from △(0)\triangle^{(0)} by uniform refinement (for κ=3\kappa=3, by a stable red-refinement rule such as that of Bey (1995), which produces finitely many similarity classes and children of equal volume), so that △1\triangle_{1} is π\pi-quasi-uniform for a fixed π\pi, and △2\triangle_{2} is obtained from △1\triangle_{1} as in Assumption B1. Let ℛα\mathcal{R}_{\alpha} be a nonempty union of simplices of △(0)\triangle^{(0)} with Vol⁡(Ω∖ℛα)>0\operatorname{Vol}(\Omega\setminus\mathcal{R}_{\alpha})>0; it is then a union of simplices of △1\triangle_{1} and of △2\triangle_{2} at every level, and it does not shrink as the mesh is refined. Let G⊆[p]G\subseteq[p] with |G|=q|G|=q and 1≤q≤p−11\leq q\leq p-1, let γℓ∗≠0\gamma^{\ast}_{\ell}\neq 0 for every ℓ\ell, so that ℐ=[p]\mathcal{I}=[p], and let bn>0b_{n}>0. Suppose that

αℓ∗=γℓ∗​bn​𝟏ℛα(ℓ∈G),αℓ∗≡0(ℓ∉G),\alpha^{\ast}_{\ell}=\gamma^{\ast}_{\ell}b_{n}\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{R}_{\alpha}}\quad(\ell\in G),\qquad\alpha^{\ast}_{\ell}\equiv 0\quad(\ell\notin G), (A.13)

with β∗\beta^{\ast} as in Assumption B2. The configuration covers plurality (2​q<p2q<p), ties (2​q=p2q=p) and strict majorities of invalid instruments (2​q>p2q>p) on ℛα\mathcal{R}_{\alpha}. Because bn>0b_{n}>0, the invalid-IV effects jump by γℓ∗​bn\gamma^{\ast}_{\ell}b_{n} at the boundary of ℛα\mathcal{R}_{\alpha}, a quantitative form of (A3). Write γmin=minℓ⁡|γℓ∗|\gamma_{\min}=\min_{\ell}|\gamma^{\ast}_{\ell}|, λ𝐙=λmin​(𝚺𝐙)>0\lambda_{\mathbf{Z}}=\lambda_{\min}(\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{Z}})>0, and M=2κ​LM=2^{\kappa L} for the number of children of a simplex of △1\triangle_{1} in △2\triangle_{2}.

Remark A.6 (Interpretation of the gap).

Proposition A.1 covers plurality, ties and strict majorities of invalid instruments on ℛα\mathcal{R}_{\alpha} in a single statement. Its gap is smaller than the gap |△|κ​n−2​c|\triangle|^{\kappa}n^{-2c} of Example A.1 by a factor |△||\triangle|. This factor is the price of comparing a perimeter with a volume. A competitor that exchanges the groups on a region of fixed size saves of order |△|−κ|\triangle|^{-\kappa} blocks but pays a loss of fit only on a transition band of order |△|−(κ−1)|\triangle|^{-(\kappa-1)} simplices. When 2​q>p2q>p, this order is attained. Take g=Q△1​φg=Q_{\triangle_{1}}\varphi with φ=bn\varphi=b_{n} on a fixed ball B⊂ℛαB\subset\mathcal{R}_{\alpha} and φ=0\varphi=0 outside its C​|△|C|\triangle|-neighborhood, and leave one valid instrument unflagged on each band simplex. The band contains of order |△|−(κ−1)|\triangle|^{-(\kappa-1)} simplices, so its loss of fit is of order bn2​|△|b_{n}^{2}|\triangle|. The roughness term satisfies ρn​ℰ​(β~+g)=O⁡(ρn+ρn​bn2​|△|−3)=o⁡(bn2​|△|)\rho_{n}\mathcal{E}(\widetilde{\beta}+g)=O(\rho_{n}+\rho_{n}b_{n}^{2}|\triangle|^{-3})=o(b_{n}^{2}|\triangle|), because ρn​|△|−4→0\rho_{n}|\triangle|^{-4}\to 0 by Assumption B7 and ρn≤en,N=o⁡(bn2​|△|κ+1)\rho_{n}\leq e_{n,N}=o(b_{n}^{2}|\triangle|^{\kappa+1}) by the tuning window. Each band simplex costs at most pp additional blocks, so the support still saves of order |△|−κ|\triangle|^{-\kappa} blocks. Hence Assumption B8(i) can hold only with ΔnG=O⁡(bn2​|△|κ+1)\Delta_{n}^{\rm G}=O(b_{n}^{2}|\triangle|^{\kappa+1}), and the exponent κ+1\kappa+1 cannot be improved in this configuration. Two features of the setting are essential. Anchoring is used in Steps 1 and 2: it guarantees an unflagged instrument on every band simplex, and this is what converts the transition band into a loss of fit rather than a change in the block count alone. The jump of size bnb_{n} at ∂ℛα\partial\mathcal{R}_{\alpha} is used in Lemma A.1. If the invalid-IV effects switched on smoothly, a smooth β\beta could follow the invalid ratio without loss, which is the non-identifiability described by Theorem 1 when (A3) fails. For general invalid-IV configurations, Assumption B8(i) remains an assumption. The proposition verifies it in a mesh-aligned idealization of the configuration used by the simulation designs, without restricting the size of ℛα\mathcal{R}_{\alpha} relative to the mesh.

Example A.3 (Rates for the anchored criterion).

With ΔnG=κ0​bn2​|△|κ+1\Delta_{n}^{\rm G}=\kappa_{0}b_{n}^{2}|\triangle|^{\kappa+1}, the tuning condition (A.12) becomes

λmax​(𝚪𝒜,λR)≤C⁡{(1+Rn,N)​|△|κ+λRn​N​|△|4−κ}.\lambda_{\max}(\bm{\Gamma}_{\mathcal{A},\lambda^{\rm R}})\leq C\left\{(1+R_{n,N})|\triangle|^{\kappa}+\frac{\lambda^{\rm R}}{nN|\triangle|^{4-\kappa}}\right\}.

Since Rn,N=oP​(1)R_{n,N}=o_{\rm P}(1), this gives the upper bound in part (b) with probability approaching one. ∎

A.2.3 Theoretical Properties of the Oracle Estimator

The oracle estimator from the main paper minimizes the smooth loss on 𝒜∗\mathcal{A}^{\ast}. In the reduced coordinates of Section A.2.1,

𝜽^o∈arg​min𝜽⁡{‖𝐘−𝐔​𝜽‖2n​N+ρn​𝜽β⊤​𝐖1​𝜽β},β^o=𝐁~1⊤​𝜽^βo.\begin{gathered}\widehat{\bm{\theta}}^{o}\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\bm{\theta}}\left\{\frac{\|\mathbf{Y}-\mathbf{U}\bm{\theta}\|^{2}}{nN}+\rho_{n}\bm{\theta}_{\beta}^{\top}\mathbf{W}_{1}\bm{\theta}_{\beta}\right\},\\ \widehat{\beta}^{o}=\widetilde{\mathbf{B}}_{1}^{\top}\widehat{\bm{\theta}}_{\beta}^{o}.\end{gathered} (A.18)

On the event of Lemma A.4, its normal equations give

𝜽^o=𝚪𝒜∗−1​𝐔⊤​𝐘n​N.\widehat{\bm{\theta}}^{o}=\bm{\Gamma}_{\mathcal{A}^{\ast}}^{-1}\frac{\mathbf{U}^{\top}\mathbf{Y}}{nN}. (A.19)

Partition 𝐔i​j=(𝐔i​j(1)⊤,𝐔i​j(2)⊤)⊤\mathbf{U}_{ij}=(\mathbf{U}_{ij}^{(1)\top},\mathbf{U}_{ij}^{(2)\top})^{\top} into its causal-effect and invalid-effect blocks, and put

𝐔a​b=∑i=1n∑j=1N𝐔i​j(a)​𝐔i​j(b)⊤,a,b∈{1,2},𝐄=1n​N∑i,j𝐔i​j(1)Yi​j,𝐅=1n​N∑i,j𝐔i​j(2)Yi​j.\begin{gathered}\mathbf{U}_{ab}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\mathbf{U}_{ij}^{(a)}\mathbf{U}_{ij}^{(b)\top},\quad a,b\in\{1,2\},\\ \mathbf{E}=\frac{1}{nN}\sum_{i,j}\mathbf{U}_{ij}^{(1)}Y_{ij},\qquad\mathbf{F}=\frac{1}{nN}\sum_{i,j}\mathbf{U}_{ij}^{(2)}Y_{ij}.\end{gathered}

For the approximation terms, let

μi​j∗=Di​β∗​(𝒔j)+𝐙i⊤​𝜶∗​(𝒔j),μ~i​j=Di​β~​(𝒔j)+𝐙i⊤​𝜶~​(𝒔j),\mu^{\ast}_{ij}=D_{i}\beta^{\ast}(\bm{s}_{j})+\mathbf{Z}_{i}^{\top}\bm{\alpha}^{\ast}(\bm{s}_{j}),\qquad\widetilde{\mu}_{ij}=D_{i}\widetilde{\beta}(\bm{s}_{j})+\mathbf{Z}_{i}^{\top}\widetilde{\bm{\alpha}}(\bm{s}_{j}),

and stack these quantities in subject order:

(A.22)

The random error is of order OP(n−1/2)O_{\mathrm{P}}(n^{-1/2}).

Lemma A.5.

Under Assumptions B1–B4 and B6, we have ‖(n​N)−1​(𝐔⊤​𝛍∗−𝐔⊤​𝛍~)‖=OP​(|△|d+1+κ/2)\|(nN)^{-1}(\mathbf{U}^{\top}\bm{\mu}^{\ast}-\mathbf{U}^{\top}\widetilde{\bm{\mu}})\|=O_{\mathrm{P}}(|\triangle|^{d+1+\kappa/2}).
