By Lemma S1.2 in Yu et al. (2021),

‖(n​N)−1​𝐔⊤​(𝝁∗−𝝁~)‖2\displaystyle\bigl\|(nN)^{-1}\mathbf{U}^{\top}(\bm{\mu}^{\ast}-\widetilde{\bm{\mu}})\bigr\|^{2}
=‖1n​N​∑i=1n∑j=1ND^i​𝐁~1​(𝒔j)​(μi​j∗−μ~i​j)‖2+∑ℓ=1p‖1n​N​∑i=1n∑j=1NZi​ℓ​𝐁2,𝒜ℓ∗⊤​(𝒔j)​(μi​j∗−μ~i​j)‖2\displaystyle\quad=\left\|\frac{1}{nN}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\widehat{D}_{i}\widetilde{\mathbf{B}}_{1}(\bm{s}_{j})(\mu_{ij}^{\ast}-\widetilde{\mu}_{ij})\right\|^{2}+\sum_{\ell=1}^{p}\left\|\frac{1}{nN}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{N}Z_{i\ell}\mathbf{B}_{2,\mathcal{A}_{\ell}^{\ast}}^{\top}(\bm{s}_{j})(\mu_{ij}^{\ast}-\widetilde{\mu}_{ij})\right\|^{2}
=OP​{|△|−κ​(|△|κ⋅|△|d+1)2+C2​∑ℓ=1p|𝒜ℓ∗|​(|△|κ⋅|△|d+1)2}\displaystyle\quad=O_{\mathrm{P}}\left\{|\triangle|^{-\kappa}(|\triangle|^{\kappa}\cdot|\triangle|^{d+1})^{2}+C_{2}\sum_{\ell=1}^{p}|\mathcal{A}_{\ell}^{\ast}|(|\triangle|^{\kappa}\cdot|\triangle|^{d+1})^{2}\right\}
=OP​(|△|2​d+2+κ).\displaystyle\quad=O_{\mathrm{P}}(|\triangle|^{2d+2+\kappa}).

Here, for the first term, write 𝐁~1=𝐐2⊤​𝐁1\widetilde{\mathbf{B}}_{1}=\mathbf{Q}_{2}^{\top}\mathbf{B}_{1} and use ‖𝐐2⊤​𝒗‖≤‖𝒗‖\|\mathbf{Q}_{2}^{\top}\bm{v}\|\leq\|\bm{v}\|, where

𝒗=(n​N)−1​∑i=1n∑j=1ND^i​𝐁1​(𝒔j)​(μi​j∗−μ~i​j).{\bm{v}=(nN)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\widehat{D}_{i}\,\mathbf{B}_{1}(\bm{s}_{j})\,(\mu^{\ast}_{ij}-\widetilde{\mu}_{ij}).}

Each of the O⁡(|△|−κ)O(|\triangle|^{-\kappa}) coordinates of 𝒗\bm{v} involves a basis function bounded by one and supported on O⁡(1)O(1) simplices, hence on O⁡(N​|△|κ)O(N|\triangle|^{\kappa}) locations by Assumption B1, and

|μi​j∗−μ~i​j|≤C​|△|d+1​(‖β∗‖d+1,∞+Cα)​(|Di|+‖𝐙i‖1){|\mu^{\ast}_{ij}-\widetilde{\mu}_{ij}|\ \leq\ C|\triangle|^{d+1}\bigl(\|\beta^{\ast}\|_{d+1,\infty}+C_{\alpha}\bigr)\bigl(|D_{i}|+\|\mathbf{Z}_{i}\|_{1}\bigr)}

by the preceding sup-norm approximation bounds (Assumptions B2 and B3), while n−1​∑i|D^i|​(|Di|+‖𝐙i‖1)=OP​(1)n^{-1}\sum_{i}|\widehat{D}_{i}|(|D_{i}|+\|\mathbf{Z}_{i}\|_{1})=O_{\mathrm{P}}(1) by Assumption B6. The second term is bounded in the same way, each 𝐁2,k\mathbf{B}_{2,k} being supported on a single simplex, with ∑ℓ|𝒜ℓ∗|=|𝒜∗|≤s0​K2=O⁡(|△|−κ)\sum_{\ell}|\mathcal{A}^{\ast}_{\ell}|=|\mathcal{A}^{\ast}|\leq s_{0}K_{2}=O(|\triangle|^{-\kappa}) coordinates (Assumption B3). The constant in the OPO_{\mathrm{P}} bound is proportional to ‖β∗‖d+1,∞+Cα\|\beta^{\ast}\|_{d+1,\infty}+C_{\alpha}. Taking square roots yields the desired result. ∎

Lemma A.6.

For the first-stage OLS fit,

‖1n​N​∑i=1n∑j=1N𝐔i​j​(Di−D^i)​𝐁~1​(𝒔j)⊤​𝜽~β‖=0.\left\|\frac{1}{nN}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\mathbf{U}_{ij}(D_{i}-\widehat{D}_{i})\widetilde{\mathbf{B}}_{1}(\bm{s}_{j})^{\top}\widetilde{\bm{\theta}}_{\beta}\right\|=0.
Proof.

Let ui:=Di−D^iu_{i}:=D_{i}-\widehat{D}_{i} be the first-stage OLS residuals from regressing DD on the instrument matrix (whose columns include ZℓZ_{\ell}). By OLS orthogonality, ∑i=1nZi​ℓ​ui=0\sum_{i=1}^{n}Z_{i\ell}u_{i}=0 for each ℓ\ell, and since D^∈span​{Z}\widehat{D}\in\mathrm{span}\{Z\} we also have ∑i=1nD^i​ui=0\sum_{i=1}^{n}\widehat{D}_{i}\,u_{i}=0.

Note that the sums over jj do not depend on ii, so we may factor them out:

1n​N​∑i=1nZi​ℓ​ui​∑j=1N𝐁2,𝒜ℓ∗​(𝒔j)​𝐁~1​(𝒔j)⊤​𝜽~β\displaystyle\frac{1}{nN}\sum_{i=1}^{n}Z_{i\ell}u_{i}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\mathbf{B}_{2,\mathcal{A}_{\ell}^{\ast}}(\bm{s}_{j})\widetilde{\mathbf{B}}_{1}(\bm{s}_{j})^{\top}\widetilde{\bm{\theta}}_{\beta}
={1n​∑i=1nZi​ℓ​ui}​{1N​∑j=1N𝐁2,𝒜ℓ∗​(𝒔j)​𝐁~1​(𝒔j)⊤​𝜽~β}=𝟎,\displaystyle=\left\{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}Z_{i\ell}u_{i}\right\}\left\{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\mathbf{B}_{2,\mathcal{A}_{\ell}^{\ast}}(\bm{s}_{j})\widetilde{\mathbf{B}}_{1}(\bm{s}_{j})^{\top}\widetilde{\bm{\theta}}_{\beta}\right\}=\mathbf{0},

and similarly

1n​N​∑i=1nD^i​ui​∑j=1N𝐁~1​(𝒔j)​𝐁~1​(𝒔j)⊤​𝜽~β\displaystyle\frac{1}{nN}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\widehat{D}_{i}u_{i}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\widetilde{\mathbf{B}}_{1}(\bm{s}_{j})\widetilde{\mathbf{B}}_{1}(\bm{s}_{j})^{\top}\widetilde{\bm{\theta}}_{\beta}
={1n​∑i=1nD^i​ui}​{1N​∑j=1N𝐁~1​(𝒔j)​𝐁~1​(𝒔j)⊤​𝜽~β}=𝟎.\displaystyle=\left\{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\widehat{D}_{i}u_{i}\right\}\left\{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\widetilde{\mathbf{B}}_{1}(\bm{s}_{j})\widetilde{\mathbf{B}}_{1}(\bm{s}_{j})^{\top}\widetilde{\bm{\theta}}_{\beta}\right\}=\mathbf{0}.

Both identities hold because the first factor in each product is zero by the OLS normal equations. ∎

Lemma A.7.

Under Assumptions B1, B4, B5 and B6, we have

‖(n​N)−1​𝐔⊤​ϵ‖\displaystyle\|(nN)^{-1}\mathbf{U}^{\top}\bm{\epsilon}\| =OP{n−1/2|△|κ/2+(nN)−1/2},\displaystyle=O_{\mathrm{P}}\{n^{-1/2}|\triangle|^{\kappa/2}+(nN)^{-1/2}\}, (A.24)
‖(n​N)−1​𝐔⊤​ϵ‖∞\displaystyle\|(nN)^{-1}\mathbf{U}^{\top}\bm{\epsilon}\|_{\infty} =OP[{n−1/2|△|κ/2+(nN)−1/2}×{logn+log(pK2)}1/2].\displaystyle=O_{\mathrm{P}}\Big[\{n^{-1/2}|\triangle|^{\kappa/2}+(nN)^{-1/2}\}\times\{\log n+\log(pK_{2})\}^{1/2}\Big]. (A.25)
Proof.

Assumption B5 gives

𝔼{ϵi(𝒔)ϵi(𝒔′)}=Gη(𝒔,𝒔′)+σε2(𝒔)𝟏{𝒔=𝒔′},\mathbb{E}\{\epsilon_{i}(\bm{s})\epsilon_{i}(\bm{s}^{\prime})\}=G_{\eta}(\bm{s},\bm{s}^{\prime})+\sigma_{\varepsilon}^{2}(\bm{s})\mathbf{1}\{\bm{s}=\bm{s}^{\prime}\},

with GηG_{\eta} square-integrable on Ω×Ω\Omega\times\Omega and σε2\sigma_{\varepsilon}^{2} bounded. Let 𝑿i=(Di0,Zi​1,⋯,Zi​p)⊤\bm{X}_{i}=({D^{0}_{i}},Z_{i1},\cdots,Z_{ip})^{\top}, 𝐛1​(𝒔j)=𝐁~1​(𝒔j)\mathbf{b}_{1}(\bm{s}_{j})=\widetilde{\mathbf{B}}_{1}(\bm{s}_{j}) and 𝐛ℓ+1​(𝒔j)=𝐁2,𝒜ℓ∗​(𝒔j)\mathbf{b}_{\ell+1}(\bm{s}_{j})=\mathbf{B}_{2,\mathcal{A}_{\ell}^{\ast}}(\bm{s}_{j}) for ℓ=1,…,p\ell=1,\ldots,p. Writing D^i=Di0+𝐙i⊤​𝜹\widehat{D}_{i}=D^{0}_{i}+\mathbf{Z}_{i}^{\top}\bm{\delta} with 𝜹=𝜸^−𝜸∗=OP(n−1/2)\bm{\delta}=\widehat{\bm{\gamma}}-\bm{\gamma}^{\ast}=O_{\mathrm{P}}(n^{-1/2}) (Assumption B6), the first block of (n​N)−1​𝐔⊤​ϵ(nN)^{-1}\mathbf{U}^{\top}\bm{\epsilon} equals (n​N)−1​∑i,jDi0​𝐛1​(𝒔j)​ϵi​j+∑ℓ=1pδℓ​(n​N)−1​∑i,jZi​ℓ​𝐛1​(𝒔j)​ϵi​j(nN)^{-1}\sum_{i,j}D^{0}_{i}\mathbf{b}_{1}(\bm{s}_{j})\epsilon_{ij}+\sum_{\ell=1}^{p}\delta_{\ell}\,(nN)^{-1}\sum_{i,j}Z_{i\ell}\mathbf{b}_{1}(\bm{s}_{j})\epsilon_{ij}. Each of these p+1p+1 sums is of the form treated below, with an ii-factor built from (Di0,𝐙i)(D^{0}_{i},\mathbf{Z}_{i}), which is independent of ϵi\bm{\epsilon}_{i} and independent across ii by Assumption B4; hence the second term is OP(n−1/2)O_{\mathrm{P}}(n^{-1/2}) times the bound obtained for the first, and it suffices to prove the lemma with Di0D^{0}_{i} in place of D^i\widehat{D}_{i}. Below, 𝐔\mathbf{U} is understood accordingly. (The factorisation of expectations used next fails for D^i\widehat{D}_{i}, which depends on the whole sample and is correlated with ϵi​j\epsilon_{ij} through ξi\xi_{i}; this is why the split is needed.) The pairs (𝑿i,ϵi)(\bm{X}_{i},\bm{\epsilon}_{i}) are independent across ii, and 𝑿i\bm{X}_{i} is independent of ϵi\bm{\epsilon}_{i} by Assumption B4. The basis vectors are deterministic, and 𝐔i​j⊤​𝐔i​j′=∑ℓ=1p+1Xi​ℓ2​𝐛ℓ​(𝒔j)⊤​𝐛ℓ​(𝒔j′)\mathbf{U}_{ij}^{\top}\mathbf{U}_{ij^{\prime}}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{p+1}X_{i\ell}^{2}\mathbf{b}_{\ell}(\bm{s}_{j})^{\top}\mathbf{b}_{\ell}(\bm{s}_{j^{\prime}}). Therefore,

𝔼​‖(n​N)−1​𝐔⊤​ϵ‖2\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigl\|(nN)^{-1}\mathbf{U}^{\top}\bm{\epsilon}\bigr\|^{2}
=(n​N)−2​∑i=1n∑ℓ=1p+1𝔼⁡(Xi​ℓ2)​∑j,j′=1N𝐛ℓ​(𝒔j)⊤​𝐛ℓ​(𝒔j′)​Gϵ​(𝒔j,𝒔j′)\displaystyle\quad=(nN)^{-2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{\ell=1}^{p+1}\mathbb{E}(X_{i\ell}^{2})\sum_{j,j^{\prime}=1}^{N}\mathbf{b}_{\ell}(\bm{s}_{j})^{\top}\mathbf{b}_{\ell}(\bm{s}_{j^{\prime}})G_{\epsilon}(\bm{s}_{j},\bm{s}_{j^{\prime}})
=(n​N)−2​∑i=1n∑ℓ=1p+1𝔼⁡(Xi​ℓ2)​{∑j,j′𝐛ℓ​(𝒔j)⊤​𝐛ℓ​(𝒔j′)​Gη​(𝒔j,𝒔j′)+∑j‖𝐛ℓ​(𝒔j)‖2​σε2​(𝒔j)}.\displaystyle\quad=(nN)^{-2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{\ell=1}^{p+1}\mathbb{E}(X_{i\ell}^{2})\Bigg\{\sum_{j,j^{\prime}}\mathbf{b}_{\ell}(\bm{s}_{j})^{\top}\mathbf{b}_{\ell}(\bm{s}_{j^{\prime}})G_{\eta}(\bm{s}_{j},\bm{s}_{j^{\prime}})+\sum_{j}\|\mathbf{b}_{\ell}(\bm{s}_{j})\|^{2}\sigma_{\varepsilon}^{2}(\bm{s}_{j})\Bigg\}.

We bound the two sums for each ℓ\ell:

∑j,j′𝐛ℓ​(𝒔j)⊤​𝐛ℓ​(𝒔j′)​Gη​(𝒔j,𝒔j′)\displaystyle\sum_{j,j^{\prime}}\mathbf{b}_{\ell}(\bm{s}_{j})^{\top}\mathbf{b}_{\ell}(\bm{s}_{j^{\prime}})G_{\eta}(\bm{s}_{j},\bm{s}_{j^{\prime}}) ≲N2​|△|κ,\displaystyle\lesssim N^{2}|\triangle|^{\kappa},
∑j‖𝐛ℓ​(𝒔j)‖2​σε2​(𝒔j)\displaystyle\sum_{j}\|\mathbf{b}_{\ell}(\bm{s}_{j})\|^{2}\sigma_{\varepsilon}^{2}(\bm{s}_{j}) ≲N.\displaystyle\lesssim N.

These bounds hold uniformly over ℓ\ell. Lemma A.12 (Bounds for the refitted losses and the mBIC penalty).

Under Assumptions B1–B7, there is a constant b0>0b_{0}>0 such that

Pr{inf𝜽F(𝜽)≥b0}⟶1,sup𝒜F𝒜≤F(𝟎)=OP(1),vn=oP(n−1).\Pr\{\inf_{\bm{\theta}}F(\bm{\theta})\geq b_{0}\}\longrightarrow 1,\qquad\sup_{\mathcal{A}}F_{\mathcal{A}}\leq F(\mathbf{0})=O_{\mathrm{P}}(1),\qquad v_{n}=o_{\rm P}(n^{-1}).

In particular, all refitted and fitted mBIC criteria are well defined with probability tending to one.

Proof.

Let HNH_{N} be the orthogonal projector onto the complement of the span of the columns of 𝔹2\mathbb{B}_{2} and the p+1p+1 sampled true coefficient functions β∗,α1∗,…,αp∗\beta^{*},\alpha_{1}^{*},\ldots,\alpha_{p}^{*}. These are deterministic spatial vectors. Since dd and pp are fixed,

rank⁡(HN)≥N−C​K2−(p+1),rank⁡(HN)N⟶1;\operatorname{rank}(H_{N})\geq N-CK_{2}-(p+1),\qquad\frac{\operatorname{rank}(H_{N})}{N}\longrightarrow 1;

the last statement follows from N​|△|κ→∞N|\triangle|^{\kappa}\to\infty in Assumption B7 and K2≍|△|−κK_{2}\asymp|\triangle|^{-\kappa}. Nesting places every fitted spatial vector in col⁡(𝔹2)\operatorname{col}(\mathbb{B}_{2}). The true mean for subject ii is Di​β∗+∑ℓZi​ℓ​αℓ∗D_{i}\beta^{*}+\sum_{\ell}Z_{i\ell}\alpha_{\ell}^{*}, so HNH_{N} annihilates it as well. Consequently, for every coefficient vector,

F⁡(𝜽)≥1n​N​∑i=1n‖HN​ϵi‖2.F(\bm{\theta})\geq\frac{1}{nN}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\|H_{N}\bm{\epsilon}_{i}\|^{2}.

The independent measurement errors in Assumptions B4–B5 give 𝐆ϵ⪰cσ2​𝐈N\mathbf{G}_{\epsilon}\succeq c_{\sigma}^{2}\mathbf{I}_{N}. Thus

𝔼⁡{‖HN​ϵi‖2N}=tr⁡(HN​𝐆ϵ)N≥cσ2​rank⁡(HN)N.\mathbb{E}\left\{\frac{\|H_{N}\bm{\epsilon}_{i}\|^{2}}{N}\right\}=\frac{\operatorname{tr}(H_{N}\mathbf{G}_{\epsilon})}{N}\geq c_{\sigma}^{2}\frac{\operatorname{rank}(H_{N})}{N}.

Equation (A.42) gives supi,j𝔼​|ϵi​j|4≤16​Kϵ4\sup_{i,j}\mathbb{E}|\epsilon_{ij}|^{4}\leq 16K_{\epsilon}^{4}. Since HNH_{N} is a contraction,

𝔼⁡{‖HN​ϵi‖4N2}≤1N2​∑j,j′𝔼⁡{ϵi2​(𝒔j)​ϵi2​(𝒔j′)}≤C.\mathbb{E}\left\{\frac{\|H_{N}\bm{\epsilon}_{i}\|^{4}}{N^{2}}\right\}\leq\frac{1}{N^{2}}\sum_{j,j^{\prime}}\mathbb{E}\{\epsilon_{i}^{2}(\bm{s}_{j})\epsilon_{i}^{2}(\bm{s}_{j^{\prime}})\}\leq C.

Independence across subjects and Chebyshev’s inequality now prove the first assertion, for example with b0=cσ2/2b_{0}=c_{\sigma}^{2}/2. This argument does not condition on the estimated first stage. The zero coefficient vector is feasible on every support, and the bounded true coefficient functions and second moments of the covariates and errors give 𝔼​{F⁡(𝟎)}≤C\mathbb{E}\{F(\mathbf{0})\}\leq C. This proves the second assertion.

For the last assertion, the covariance matrix is positive semidefinite and the independent nugget makes each within-simplex correlation sum positive. Since each correlation is at most one, Neff,k≥1N_{\mathrm{eff},k}\geq 1, and hence qn≥n​K2q_{n}\geq nK_{2}. For all sufficiently large nn, x↦(log⁡x)/xx\mapsto(\log x)/x is decreasing on [n​K2,∞)[nK_{2},\infty), so

n​vn0≤log⁡(n​K2)+2​a0​log⁡(p​K2)K2⟶0.nv_{n}^{0}\leq\frac{\log(nK_{2})+2a_{0}\log(pK_{2})}{K_{2}}\longrightarrow 0.

Indeed, n1/2​|△|d+1→0n^{1/2}|\triangle|^{d+1}\to 0 implies K2/nκ/(2​d+2)→∞K_{2}/n^{\kappa/(2d+2)}\to\infty, while log⁡K2/K2→0\log K_{2}/K_{2}\to 0. Proposition A.3 (Consistency of mBIC on a global SCAD path).

Fix a deterministic roughness-parameter sequence λR>0\lambda^{\rm R}>0 and let Λn⊂(0,∞)\Lambda_{n}\subset(0,\infty) be a finite deterministic grid. The grid may depend on n,Nn,N. Suppose it contains a deterministic point λ~S\widetilde{\lambda}^{\rm S} at which Assumptions B1–B8 hold, and that

en,N=o⁡{(λminS)2},λminS=min⁡Λn.e_{n,N}=o\{(\lambda_{\min}^{\rm S})^{2}\},\qquad\lambda_{\min}^{\rm S}=\min\Lambda_{n}. (A.45)

At every λS∈Λn\lambda^{\rm S}\in\Lambda_{n}, let 𝛉^λS\widehat{\bm{\theta}}_{\lambda^{\rm S}} be a global minimizer of (6) under (7), with the same λR\lambda^{\rm R} and pilot estimate q^n\widehat{q}_{n} throughout. If λ^S\widehat{\lambda}^{\rm S} minimizes mBICλS\operatorname{mBIC}_{\lambda^{\rm S}} over Λn\Lambda_{n}, then

Pr{𝒜λ^S=𝒜∗,𝜽^λ^S=𝜽^orc}⟶1.\Pr\left\{\mathcal{A}_{\widehat{\lambda}^{\rm S}}=\mathcal{A}^{\ast},\quad\widehat{\bm{\theta}}_{\widehat{\lambda}^{\rm S}}=\widehat{\bm{\theta}}^{\,\mathrm{orc}}\right\}\longrightarrow 1.

There is no upper bound on the grid values and no restriction on the rate at which the finite grid’s cardinality grows.

Proof.

The block-curvature bound in the proof of Proposition A.2 is C​|△|κ<kaC|\triangle|^{\kappa}<k_{a} for all sufficiently large nn and does not depend on λS\lambda^{\rm S}. Lemma A.9 therefore applies simultaneously to every positive grid value. Write λ=λS\lambda=\lambda^{\rm S} and C𝒜​(λ)=F𝒜+ca​λ2​|𝒜|C_{\mathcal{A}}(\lambda)=F_{\mathcal{A}}+c_{a}\lambda^{2}|\mathcal{A}|. Every global fit has only zero or SCAD-flat blocks. minℬ⁡Cℬ​(λ)\displaystyle\min_{\mathcal{B}}C_{\mathcal{B}}(\lambda) =Qλ​(𝜽^λ)=F⁡(𝜽^λ)+ca​λ2​|𝒜|≥C𝒜​(λ)≥minℬ⁡Cℬ​(λ).\displaystyle=Q_{\lambda}(\widehat{\bm{\theta}}_{\lambda})=F(\widehat{\bm{\theta}}_{\lambda})+c_{a}\lambda^{2}|\mathcal{A}|\geq C_{\mathcal{A}}(\lambda)\geq\min_{\mathcal{B}}C_{\mathcal{B}}(\lambda).

All inequalities are equalities. In particular, 𝒜\mathcal{A} minimizes Cℬ​(λ)C_{\mathcal{B}}(\lambda) and F⁡(𝜽^λ)=F𝒜F(\widehat{\bm{\theta}}_{\lambda})=F_{\mathcal{A}}.

Next, the common refit bounds (A.39) imply, for every |𝒜|>sn∗|\mathcal{A}|>s_{n}^{\ast} and every grid value,

C𝒜​(λ)−C𝒜∗​(λ)≥ca​(λminS)2​(|𝒜|−sn∗)−Rn>0C_{\mathcal{A}}(\lambda)-C_{\mathcal{A}^{\ast}}(\lambda)\geq c_{a}(\lambda_{\min}^{\rm S})^{2}(|\mathcal{A}|-s_{n}^{\ast})-R_{n}>0

with probability tending to one, where the same Rn=OP​(en,N)R_{n}=O_{\mathrm{P}}(e_{n,N}) works for all supports and all grid values. Condition (A.45) makes the final inequality strict on a single event. Hence every grid fit has at most sn∗s_{n}^{\ast} active blocks on that event.

Proposition A.2 gives the oracle fit at λ~S\widetilde{\lambda}^{\rm S} with probability tending to one. Intersect this event with the preceding events and the event in Lemma A.13. The equality between each global fit’s loss and its refitted loss gives

mBIC𝒜λ^S=mBICλ^S≤mBICλ~S=mBIC𝒜∗.\operatorname{mBIC}_{\mathcal{A}_{\widehat{\lambda}^{\rm S}}}=\operatorname{mBIC}_{\widehat{\lambda}^{\rm S}}\leq\operatorname{mBIC}_{\widetilde{\lambda}^{\rm S}}=\operatorname{mBIC}_{\mathcal{A}^{\ast}}.

Since |𝒜λ^S|≤sn∗|\mathcal{A}_{\widehat{\lambda}^{\rm S}}|\leq s_{n}^{\ast}, the strict ordering in (A.44) forces 𝒜λ^S=𝒜∗\mathcal{A}_{\widehat{\lambda}^{\rm S}}=\mathcal{A}^{\ast}. Finally, the selected fit minimizes FF on this support. The oracle quadratic refit is unique on the event of Lemma A.4(b), so the selected coefficient vector equals 𝜽^orc\widehat{\bm{\theta}}^{\,\mathrm{orc}}. The intersection of these finitely many common events has probability tending to one, regardless of the number of grid points. ∎

The grid restriction is compatible with the existing global conditions. For the rates in Example A.1, en,N≍n−1e_{n,N}\asymp n^{-1} and λ~S=n−1/3\widetilde{\lambda}^{\rm S}=n^{-1/3}. Any finite deterministic grid containing n−1/3n^{-1/3} and contained in [n−2/5,∞)[n^{-2/5},\infty) satisfies (A.45), since n−1=o(n−4/5)n^{-1}=o(n^{-4/5}). Grid points above λ~S\widetilde{\lambda}^{\rm S} need not satisfy the upper tuning bound in Assumption B8; their fits may omit true blocks. The comparison in Lemma A.13 excludes these fits from the selected solution.

Model-size control.

We first bound the projection of the error onto one simplex. We then add invalid-IV blocks one at a time and sum their residual projections. Finally, we compare each support with its union with the true support. All norms below are Euclidean norms. The normalization by n​NnN is included when comparing a squared projection with the loss FF.

Let d0=(d+κκ)d_{0}=\binom{d+\kappa}{\kappa}, and let 𝚷k\bm{\Pi}_{k} project onto the sampled degree-dd polynomials supported on TkT_{k}. Assign observations on shared faces to one simplex, as for the broken basis. Put

𝐐k=𝐏Z⊗𝚷k,Mn=maxk≤K2⁡‖𝐐k​ϵ‖2,\mathbf{Q}_{k}=\mathbf{P}_{Z}\otimes\bm{\Pi}_{k},\qquad M_{n}=\max_{k\leq K_{2}}\|\mathbf{Q}_{k}\bm{\epsilon}\|^{2},

where 𝐏Z\mathbf{P}_{Z} projects onto col⁡(𝐙)\operatorname{col}(\mathbf{Z}). The spaces col⁡(𝐐k)\operatorname{col}(\mathbf{Q}_{k}) are mutually orthogonal and contain all instrument-polynomial columns on their simplices.

For any support ℬ\mathcal{B}, block b∉ℬb\notin\mathcal{B} and 𝒈∈𝒢n\bm{g}\in\mathcal{G}_{n}, define the augmented residual and its projector by

𝐑b|ℬ​(𝒈)={𝐈−𝐏ℬ​(𝒈)}​𝐉𝐔α,b,𝚷b|ℬ​(𝒈)=proj⁡{col⁡(𝐑b|ℬ​(𝒈))}.\mathbf{R}_{b\mid\mathcal{B}}(\bm{g})=\{\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{P}_{\mathcal{B}}(\bm{g})\}\mathbf{J}\mathbf{U}_{\alpha,b},\qquad\bm{\Pi}_{b\mid\mathcal{B}}(\bm{g})=\operatorname{proj}\{\operatorname{col}(\mathbf{R}_{b\mid\mathcal{B}}(\bm{g}))\}.

For an ordering E={b1,…,bs}⊆𝒜cE=\{b_{1},\ldots,b_{s}\}\subseteq\mathcal{A}^{c}, set 𝒜j=𝒜∪{b1,…,bj}\mathcal{A}_{j}=\mathcal{A}\cup\{b_{1},\ldots,b_{j}\} and 𝒜0=𝒜\mathcal{A}_{0}=\mathcal{A}. Then

𝐏𝒜∪E​(𝒈)−𝐏𝒜​(𝒈)=∑j=1s𝚷bj|𝒜j−1​(𝒈),\mathbf{P}_{\mathcal{A}\cup E}(\bm{g})-\mathbf{P}_{\mathcal{A}}(\bm{g})=\sum_{j=1}^{s}\bm{\Pi}_{b_{j}\mid\mathcal{A}_{j-1}}(\bm{g}), (A.46)

and the summands are mutually orthogonal projectors.

Lemma A.14 (Local noise and nested projections).

Under Assumptions B1 and B4–B6, Mn=OP​{(N/K2)​log⁡(e​P0)}M_{n}=O_{\mathrm{P}}\{(N/K_{2})\log(eP_{0})\}. If also |△|→0|\triangle|\to 0, then there is a fixed constant CMC_{M} such that, with probability tending to one,

‖𝐐k​ϵ‖2n​N≤CM​log⁡(e​P0)n​K2​Neff,k(k≤K2),Mnn​N≤CM​log⁡(e​P0)qn,\frac{\|\mathbf{Q}_{k}\bm{\epsilon}\|^{2}}{nN}\leq\frac{C_{M}\log(eP_{0})}{nK_{2}N_{\mathrm{eff},k}}\quad(k\leq K_{2}),\qquad\frac{M_{n}}{nN}\leq\frac{C_{M}\log(eP_{0})}{q_{n}}, (A.47)

where CMC_{M} may be enlarged for the second inequality.

Suppose the following locality bound holds on one event of probability tending to one, uniformly over the comparisons under consideration and 𝐠∈𝒢n\bm{g}\in\mathcal{G}_{n}. For each b=(ℓ,k)b=(\ell,k), there are nested unions ωt​(Tk)\omega_{t}(T_{k}) of at most Cω​(t+1)κC_{\omega}(t+1)^{\kappa} fine simplices, containing TkT_{k}, such that

‖𝐃ωtc​𝐉⊤​𝚷b|ℬ​(𝒈)‖op≤C0​ϑt+1,t≥0,\|\mathbf{D}_{\omega_{t}^{c}}\mathbf{J}^{\top}\bm{\Pi}_{b\mid\mathcal{B}}(\bm{g})\|_{\rm op}\leq C_{0}\vartheta^{t+1},\qquad t\geq 0, (A.48)

with fixed C0,Cω<∞C_{0},C_{\omega}<\infty and 0<ϑ<10<\vartheta<1. Here 𝐃ωtc\mathbf{D}_{\omega_{t}^{c}} retains all subjects’ data outside ωt​(Tk)\omega_{t}(T_{k}). There is a fixed CL<∞C_{L}<\infty, depending only on the locality constants and κ\kappa, such that, on this event,

‖{𝐏𝒜∪E​(𝒈)−𝐏𝒜​(𝒈)}​𝐉​ϵ‖2≤CL2​|E|​Mn.\|\{\mathbf{P}_{\mathcal{A}\cup E}(\bm{g})-\mathbf{P}_{\mathcal{A}}(\bm{g})\}\mathbf{J}\bm{\epsilon}\|^{2}\leq C_{L}^{2}|E|M_{n}. (A.49)

Consequently, the normalized gain is at most C1​|E|​log⁡(e​P0)/qnC_{1}|E|\log(eP_{0})/q_{n}, simultaneously over those comparisons, with probability tending to one and fixed C1C_{1}. The same statements hold for ordinary projections by omitting the roughness rows and taking 𝐉=𝐈\mathbf{J}=\mathbf{I}. For ordinary projections with the unconstrained causal Bernstein basis, no additional locality condition is needed.

Proof.

Step 1: noise on a single simplex. Conditional on 𝐙\mathbf{Z}, independence of the KL scores and nugget variables gives, for every fixed 𝐯\mathbf{v} and u∈ℝu\in\mathbb{R},

𝔼⁡{eu​𝐯⊤​ϵ∣𝐙}≤exp⁡{Ksg2​u2​𝐯⊤​𝚺ϵ​𝐯/2},Ksg2=max⁡(σζ2,σe2).\mathbb{E}\{e^{u\mathbf{v}^{\top}\bm{\epsilon}}\mid\mathbf{Z}\}\leq\exp\{K_{\rm sg}^{2}u^{2}\mathbf{v}^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}_{\epsilon}\mathbf{v}/2\},\qquad K_{\rm sg}^{2}=\max(\sigma_{\zeta}^{2},\sigma_{e}^{2}). (A.50)

The infinite KL sum follows from its finite sums by L2L^{2} convergence and Fatou’s lemma along an almost surely convergent subsequence. On one simplex the covariance has trace at most Cϵ​mkC_{\epsilon}m_{k}. Thus every unit vector in col⁡(𝐐k)\operatorname{col}(\mathbf{Q}_{k}) has variance at most Cϵ​mkC_{\epsilon}m_{k}. That space has dimension at most p​d0pd_{0}, a fixed number. A 1/21/2-net of its unit sphere has at most 5p​d05^{pd_{0}} points, and its largest absolute noise score is at least ‖𝐐k​ϵ‖/2\|\mathbf{Q}_{k}\bm{\epsilon}\|/2. The sub-Gaussian bound and a union bound over the nets and simplices prove the first assertion.

To retain Neff,kN_{\mathrm{eff},k}, use the fixed covariance kernel on compact Ω\Omega. Put GM​(𝒔,𝒔′)=∑t≤Mρt​ψt​(𝒔)​ψt​(𝒔′)G_{M}(\bm{s},\bm{s}^{\prime})=\sum_{t\leq M}\rho_{t}\psi_{t}(\bm{s})\psi_{t}(\bm{s}^{\prime}). A finite subcover and continuity give fixed MM and δ>0\delta>0 such that GM​(𝒔,𝒔′)≥cG/4G_{M}(\bm{s},\bm{s}^{\prime})\geq c_{G}/4 whenever ‖𝒔−𝒔′‖≤δ\|\bm{s}-\bm{s}^{\prime}\|\leq\delta. ∑j,j′∈Tk|Gϵ​(𝒔j,𝒔j′)|≤Cϵ​mk2≤4​Cϵ2cG​Sk.\displaystyle\sum_{j,j^{\prime}\in T_{k}}|G_{\epsilon}(\bm{s}_{j},\bm{s}_{j^{\prime}})|\leq C_{\epsilon}m_{k}^{2}\leq\frac{4C_{\epsilon}^{2}}{c_{G}}S_{k}.

Then

𝔼⁡{(𝐮⊤​ϵ)2∣𝐙}\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\{(\mathbf{u}^{\top}\bm{\epsilon})^{2}\mid\mathbf{Z}\} =‖𝐚‖2​∑j,j′∈Tkf⁡(𝒔j)​f​(𝒔j′)​Gϵ​(𝒔j,𝒔j′)≤C​‖𝐚‖2​mk2Neff,k,\displaystyle=\|\mathbf{a}\|^{2}\sum_{j,j^{\prime}\in T_{k}}f(\bm{s}_{j})f(\bm{s}_{j^{\prime}})G_{\epsilon}(\bm{s}_{j},\bm{s}_{j^{\prime}})\leq C\|\mathbf{a}\|^{2}\frac{m_{k}^{2}}{N_{\mathrm{eff},k}},

The bound extends to signed polynomial contrasts. By Assumption B1 and polynomial norm equivalence, maxj∈Tk⁡|h⁡(𝒔j)|2≤C​mk−1​∑j∈Tkh​(𝒔j)2\max_{j\in T_{k}}|h(\bm{s}_{j})|^{2}\leq Cm_{k}^{-1}\sum_{j\in T_{k}}h(\bm{s}_{j})^{2} for h∈𝒫d​(Tk)h\in\mathcal{P}_{d}(T_{k}). The same net argument now gives, for x>0x>0,

Take x=2​log⁡(e​P0)x=2\log(eP_{0}), use mk≍N/K2m_{k}\asymp N/K_{2} and Neff−≥c0​N¯effN^{-}_{\mathrm{eff}}\geq c_{0}\bar{N}_{\mathrm{eff}}, and divide by n​NnN. This proves (A.47) with a fixed constant.

Step 2: add blocks in a nested order. The enlarged design space is the orthogonal sum of the current space and the span of the added residual. Hence 𝐏ℬ∪{b}−𝐏ℬ=𝚷b|ℬ\mathbf{P}_{\mathcal{B}\cup\{b\}}-\mathbf{P}_{\mathcal{B}}=\bm{\Pi}_{b\mid\mathcal{B}}, also for singular designs. Successive increments have mutually orthogonal ranges. This proves (A.46) and

‖{𝐏𝒜∪E−𝐏𝒜}​𝐉​ϵ‖2=∑j=1|E|‖𝚷bj|𝒜j−1​𝐉​ϵ‖2.\|\{\mathbf{P}_{\mathcal{A}\cup E}-\mathbf{P}_{\mathcal{A}}\}\mathbf{J}\bm{\epsilon}\|^{2}=\sum_{j=1}^{|E|}\|\bm{\Pi}_{b_{j}\mid\mathcal{A}_{j-1}}\mathbf{J}\bm{\epsilon}\|^{2}.

The sign is enlarged projector minus smaller projector.

Step 3: apply the local bound to residuals. Let 𝐯\mathbf{v} be any unit vector in a one-block residual space. Its data part 𝐯0=𝐉⊤​𝐯\mathbf{v}_{0}=\mathbf{J}^{\top}\mathbf{v} lies in ⨁kcol⁡(𝐐k)\bigoplus_{k}\operatorname{col}(\mathbf{Q}_{k}) and has norm at most one. On shell ωt∖ωt−1\omega_{t}\setminus\omega_{t-1}, its norm is at most max⁡(1,C0)​ϑt\max(1,C_{0})\vartheta^{t}, with ω−1=∅\omega_{-1}=\emptyset. Cauchy–Schwarz on each shell gives

∑k|𝐐k​𝐯0|≤max⁡(1,C0)​Cω​∑t≥0(t+1)κ/2​ϑt=:CL<∞.\sum_{k}\|\mathbf{Q}_{k}\mathbf{v}_{0}\|\leq\max(1,C_{0})\sqrt{C_{\omega}}\sum_{t\geq 0}(t+1)^{\kappa/2}\vartheta^{t}=:C_{L}<\infty.

The tail condition leaves no component outside the union of these shells. Consequently, |𝐯⊤​𝐉​ϵ|≤CL​Mn|\mathbf{v}^{\top}\mathbf{J}\bm{\epsilon}|\leq C_{L}\sqrt{M_{n}}. Taking the supremum over unit residual vectors, and then summing the nested increments, proves (A.49). The same event works for every support, order and 𝒈\bm{g}; no further union bound is needed. In the ordinary unconstrained causal space, a residual is supported on its coarse parent simplex, which contains only a fixed number of fine simplices. The preceding bound then follows directly. All stochastic conditioning was on 𝐙\mathbf{Z}. In particular, the result applies to 𝜸^\widehat{\bm{\gamma}} when it belongs to 𝒢n\mathcal{G}_{n}, even though it can depend on ϵ\bm{\epsilon}. ∎

Locality of the residuals.

Positivity of an original spline column does not imply positivity of its residual: projecting 𝐞1\mathbf{e}_{1} off the constant vector leaves 𝐞1−𝟏/M\mathbf{e}_{1}-\mathbf{1}/M, with negative entries outside its original support. The preceding argument needs only a bound on the sizes of residual tails. The following lemma gives such a bound.

Lemma A.15 (Decay outside a simplex neighborhood).

For a one-block addition b=(ℓ,k)b=(\ell,k), project out the current invalid-IV columns first. Their projector is

𝐋ℬ=∑j𝐏Zℬ⁡(j)⊗𝚷j.\mathbf{L}_{\mathcal{B}}=\sum_{j}\mathbf{P}_{Z_{\mathcal{B}(j)}}\otimes\bm{\Pi}_{j}.

For a sampled causal basis 𝐂=(c1,…,cM)\mathbf{C}=(c_{1},\ldots,c_{M}), put

𝐇0=(𝐈−𝐋ℬ)​(𝐙​𝒈⊗𝐂),𝐕b=(𝐈−𝐋ℬ)​𝐔α,b,𝐇=(𝐇0λR​𝐑C),\mathbf{H}_{0}=(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{L}_{\mathcal{B}})(\mathbf{Z}\bm{g}\otimes\mathbf{C}),\quad\mathbf{V}_{b}=(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{L}_{\mathcal{B}})\mathbf{U}_{\alpha,b},\quad\mathbf{H}=\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{H}_{0}\\ \sqrt{\lambda^{\rm R}}\mathbf{R}_{C}\end{pmatrix},

where 𝐑C\mathbf{R}_{C} is the roughness factor in the original augmented rows after the basis change, so 𝐑C⊤​𝐑C=𝐖C\mathbf{R}_{C}^{\top}\mathbf{R}_{C}=\mathbf{W}_{C}. Then 𝐑b|ℬ=(𝐈−𝐏H)​𝐉𝐕b\mathbf{R}_{b\mid\mathcal{B}}=(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{P}_{H})\mathbf{J}\mathbf{V}_{b}. Join basis indices whose supports meet a common fine simplex, and let ωt​(Tk)\omega_{t}(T_{k}) consist of the fine simplices meeting supports at graph distance at most tt from the supports meeting TkT_{k}. For 𝐆=𝐇⊤​𝐇≠0\mathbf{G}=\mathbf{H}^{\top}\mathbf{H}\neq 0, let 0<aG≤bG0<a_{G}\leq b_{G} bound its positive spectrum and put q=(bG−aG)/(bG+aG)<1q=(b_{G}-a_{G})/(b_{G}+a_{G})<1. Then

‖𝐃ωtc​𝐉⊤​𝐑b|ℬ​𝒄‖≤qt+1​‖𝐕b​𝒄‖.\|\mathbf{D}_{\omega_{t}^{c}}\mathbf{J}^{\top}\mathbf{R}_{b\mid\mathcal{B}}\bm{c}\|\leq q^{t+1}\|\mathbf{V}_{b}\bm{c}\|. (A.51)

If, additionally,

‖𝐑b|ℬ​𝒄‖≥η​‖𝐕b​𝒄‖for every ​𝒄,η>0,\|\mathbf{R}_{b\mid\mathcal{B}}\bm{c}\|\geq\eta\|\mathbf{V}_{b}\bm{c}\|\quad\text{for every }\bm{c},\qquad\eta>0, (A.52)

then the left side of (A.48) is at most η−1​qt+1\eta^{-1}q^{t+1}. When 𝐆=0\mathbf{G}=0, take q=0q=0; the residual has support on TkT_{k}.

Proof.

Let τ=2/(aG+bG)\tau=2/(a_{G}+b_{G}) and pt​(𝐆)=τ​∑j=0t(𝐈−τ​𝐆)jp_{t}(\mathbf{G})=\tau\sum_{j=0}^{t}(\mathbf{I}-\tau\mathbf{G})^{j}. Singular-value decomposition gives

‖𝐏H−𝐇​pt​(𝐆)​𝐇⊤‖op≤qt+1.\|\mathbf{P}_{H}-\mathbf{H}p_{t}(\mathbf{G})\mathbf{H}^{\top}\|_{\rm op}\leq q^{t+1}.

Indeed, the difference has eigenvalue (1−τ​λ)t+1(1-\tau\lambda)^{t+1} on an eigenvector with positive Gram eigenvalue λ\lambda, and zero on the orthogonal complement of col⁡(𝐇)\operatorname{col}(\mathbf{H}). The data columns of 𝐇\mathbf{H} retain the support of their causal basis functions. Both 𝐇0⊤​𝐇0\mathbf{H}_{0}^{\top}\mathbf{H}_{0} and 𝐖C\mathbf{W}_{C} have zero entries between nonadjacent indices; for the latter this follows from the integrals defining the roughness penalty. Thus pt​(𝐆)p_{t}(\mathbf{G}) spreads 𝐇0⊤​𝐕b\mathbf{H}_{0}^{\top}\mathbf{V}_{b} by at most tt graph steps. The data part of 𝐇​pt​(𝐆)​𝐇⊤​𝐉𝐕b\mathbf{H}p_{t}(\mathbf{G})\mathbf{H}^{\top}\mathbf{J}\mathbf{V}_{b} vanishes outside ωt​(Tk)\omega_{t}(T_{k}), as does 𝐕b\mathbf{V}_{b} itself. The operator bound proves (A.51). Dividing by the residual norm using (A.52) proves the normalized bound. No local square root of 𝐖C\mathbf{W}_{C} is required. The zero Gram case is immediate. ∎

For completeness, uniform constants follow on any family of enlarged supports satisfying (S) in Lemma A.3 with a common margin, provided the causal space has a basis of support diameter O⁡(|△|)O(|\triangle|) satisfying

c​N​|△|κ​‖𝒗‖2≤‖𝐂​𝒗‖2≤C​N​|△|κ​‖𝒗‖2.cN|\triangle|^{\kappa}\|\bm{v}\|^{2}\leq\|\mathbf{C}\bm{v}\|^{2}\leq CN|\triangle|^{\kappa}\|\bm{v}\|^{2}. (A.53)

Condition (S) gives c​n≤‖𝐰j‖2≤C​ncn\leq\|\mathbf{w}_{j}\|^{2}\leq Cn uniformly over 𝒈∈𝒢n\bm{g}\in\mathcal{G}_{n}. Since 𝐇0⊤​𝐇0=∑j‖𝐰j‖2​𝐂j⊤​𝐂j\mathbf{H}_{0}^{\top}\mathbf{H}_{0}=\sum_{j}\|\mathbf{w}_{j}\|^{2}\mathbf{C}_{j}^{\top}\mathbf{C}_{j} and ‖𝐖C‖op≤C​|△|κ−4\|\mathbf{W}_{C}\|_{\rm op}\leq C|\triangle|^{\kappa-4} by the polynomial inverse inequality, Assumption B7 gives

c​n​N​|△|κ​𝐈⪯𝐆⪯C​n​N​|△|κ​𝐈.cnN|\triangle|^{\kappa}\mathbf{I}\preceq\mathbf{G}\preceq CnN|\triangle|^{\kappa}\mathbf{I}.

Thus qq is bounded away from one. The empirical norm comparison under (S) for the enlarged support gives

‖𝐑b|ℬ​𝒄‖2≥inf𝒗‖𝐔α,b​𝒄−𝐔ℬ​(𝒈)​𝒗‖2≥c​n​N​|△|κ​‖𝒄‖2,‖𝐕b​𝒄‖2≤C​n​N​|△|κ​‖𝒄‖2.\|\mathbf{R}_{b\mid\mathcal{B}}\bm{c}\|^{2}\geq\inf_{\bm{v}}\|\mathbf{U}_{\alpha,b}\bm{c}-\mathbf{U}_{\mathcal{B}}(\bm{g})\bm{v}\|^{2}\geq cnN|\triangle|^{\kappa}\|\bm{c}\|^{2},\qquad\|\mathbf{V}_{b}\bm{c}\|^{2}\leq CnN|\triangle|^{\kappa}\|\bm{c}\|^{2}.

This supplies a uniform η>0\eta>0. Quasi-uniformity bounds the number of simplices in ωt\omega_{t} by C​(t+1)κC(t+1)^{\kappa}. These are sufficient conditions for (A.48). They are not automatic for every candidate: enlarging the true support can violate (S), and approximation power in Assumption B2 alone does not supply (A.53). For unrestricted support comparisons, the required uniform locality or covariance bound must be stated.

Lemma A.16 (Gain from adding invalid-IV blocks).

Suppose Assumptions B1–B7 hold. If (A.48) holds uniformly for every chain from 𝒜∗\mathcal{A}^{\ast} to 𝒜∗∪E\mathcal{A}^{\ast}\cup E, E⊆(𝒜∗)cE\subseteq(\mathcal{A}^{\ast})^{c}, then, with probability tending to one,

0≤F𝒜∗−F𝒜∗∪E≤Cg​|E|​log⁡(e​P0)qn+Rnbfor every ​E⊆(𝒜∗)c,0\leq F_{\mathcal{A}^{\ast}}-F_{\mathcal{A}^{\ast}\cup E}\leq C_{g}|E|\frac{\log(eP_{0})}{q_{n}}+R_{n}^{\rm b}\quad\text{for every }E\subseteq(\mathcal{A}^{\ast})^{c}, (A.54)

where CgC_{g} is fixed and the same nonnegative remainder satisfies Rnb=OP​(|△|2​d+2+ρn)R_{n}^{\rm b}=O_{\mathrm{P}}(|\triangle|^{2d+2}+\rho_{n}).

Write 𝐃E​(𝐠)=𝐏𝒜∗∪E​(𝐠)−𝐏𝒜∗​(𝐠)\mathbf{D}_{E}(\bm{g})=\mathbf{P}_{\mathcal{A}^{\ast}\cup E}(\bm{g})-\mathbf{P}_{\mathcal{A}^{\ast}}(\bm{g}). On a 𝐙\mathbf{Z}-measurable event of probability tending to one, suppose there are 𝐙\mathbf{Z}-measurable matrices 𝐇b⪰0\mathbf{H}_{b}\succeq 0 such that, simultaneously for all EE and 𝐠∈𝒢n\bm{g}\in\mathcal{G}_{n},

Finally, Proposition A.2 gives the unique oracle fit at λ~S\widetilde{\lambda}^{\rm S}. A feasible fit on actual support 𝒜\mathcal{A} has loss at least F𝒜F_{\mathcal{A}}. Hence, on the intersection of the preceding events,

mBIC𝒜λ^S≤mBICλ^S≤mBICλ~S=mBIC𝒜∗.\operatorname{mBIC}_{\mathcal{A}_{\widehat{\lambda}^{\rm S}}}\leq\operatorname{mBIC}_{\widehat{\lambda}^{\rm S}}\leq\operatorname{mBIC}_{\widetilde{\lambda}^{\rm S}}=\operatorname{mBIC}_{\mathcal{A}^{\ast}}.

Strict ordering forces the selected support to be 𝒜∗\mathcal{A}^{\ast} and its loss to equal F𝒜∗F_{\mathcal{A}^{\ast}}. Uniqueness of the oracle quadratic refit then forces equality of the coefficient vectors. Since all comparisons hold simultaneously over supports, no union bound over the tuning grid is needed. ∎

The additional conditions have separate roles. Condition (M1) controls residual noise; local support of the original basis alone does not establish it. Condition (M2) excludes the mechanism by which a representation with many invalid-IV blocks can reproduce the fitted values of a smooth β\beta while saving the entire roughness penalty, at a complexity cost of only O⁡(K2​vn)=oP​(ρn)O(K_{2}v_{n})=o_{\rm P}(\rho_{n}). Condition (M3) supplies the signal comparison for larger models outside the comparison family of Assumption B8, and (M4) makes the penalty dominate the noise gain per net added block. The result uses a fixed deterministic roughness sequence; it does not cover its later selection by cross-validation.

Remark B.1.

Conditions (C1)–(C2) are the prices of estimating the first stage and the error covariance in the variance, with the bounds available here. Step 2 of the proof of Lemma A.11 gives maxj,j′⁡|G^ϵ−Gϵ|=OP​(log⁡N/n+ϱn)\max_{j,j^{\prime}}|\widehat{G}_{\epsilon}-G_{\epsilon}|=O_{\mathrm{P}}(\sqrt{\log N/n}+\varrho_{n}), where ϱn\varrho_{n} in (A.10) is the sup-norm error of (β^,𝜶^)(\widehat{\beta},\widehat{\bm{\alpha}}); on the event {𝒜^=𝒜∗}\{\widehat{\mathcal{A}}=\mathcal{A}^{\ast}\} these are the oracle estimators, so Theorem A.1 and Corollary A.1 with an=rn,Na_{n}=r_{n,N} give ϱn=OP(|△|−κ/2rn,N)\varrho_{n}=O_{\mathrm{P}}(|\triangle|^{-\kappa/2}r_{n,N}). A sufficient condition for (C2) is therefore log⁡N/n+|△|−κ/2rn,N=o(|△|κ)\sqrt{\log N/n}+|\triangle|^{-\kappa/2}r_{n,N}=o(|\triangle|^{\kappa}), which for rn,N≍n−1/2r_{n,N}\asymp n^{-1/2} reads n​|△|3​κ→∞n|\triangle|^{3\kappa}\to\infty. This is stronger than (C1), and for κ=3\kappa=3 it is compatible with (U1) only when d≥6d\geq 6; for example, κ=3\kappa=3, d=6d=6, |△|≍n−1/10|\triangle|\asymp n^{-1/10}, N≍nN\asymp n, λR≍1\lambda^{\rm R}\asymp 1, λS≍n−1/10\lambda^{\rm S}\asymp n^{-1/10} and c<1/10c<1/10 satisfy Assumptions B3, B7, B9, (C1) and this sufficient condition for (C2), whereas in the regime given after Assumption B9 (d=5d=5, |△|≍n−1/7|\triangle|\asymp n^{-1/7}) condition (C2) does not follow from the bounds available and remains an assumption. Both (C1) and the factor |△|κ|\triangle|^{\kappa} in (C2) can be removed under a bound on the entries of 𝚪𝒜∗,λR−1\bm{\Gamma}^{-1}_{\mathcal{A}^{\ast},\lambda^{\rm R}} in the locally supported basis; see the remark after Assumption B9.

Section C. Additional Simulation Results

This section provides the complete data-generating mechanisms, implementation details, and additional numerical summaries for the simulation studies in the main paper.

C.1 Data-generating mechanisms

C.1.1 Common model

For subject i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n and spatial location 𝒔j∈Ω\bm{s}_{j}\in\Omega, the data are generated from

Yi​(𝒔j)=Di​β∗​(𝒔j)+𝒁i⊤​𝜶∗​(𝒔j)+ηi​(𝒔j)+εi​(𝒔j),Di=𝒁i⊤​𝜸∗+ξi.\displaystyle Y_{i}(\bm{s}_{j})=D_{i}\beta^{\ast}(\bm{s}_{j})+\bm{Z}_{i}^{\top}\bm{\alpha}^{\ast}(\bm{s}_{j})+\eta_{i}(\bm{s}_{j})+\varepsilon_{i}(\bm{s}_{j}),\quad D_{i}=\bm{Z}_{i}^{\top}\bm{\gamma}^{\ast}+\xi_{i}.

We consider n∈{100,300}n\in\{100,300\} and p∈{3,10}p\in\{3,10\}. The instruments are generated as

𝒁i∼Np​(𝟎,σZ2​𝐈p),𝜸∗={𝟏p,p=3,0.6​ 1p,p=10.\bm{Z}_{i}\sim N_{p}(\bm{0},\sigma_{Z}^{2}\mathbf{I}_{p}),\qquad\bm{\gamma}^{\ast}=\begin{cases}\mathbf{1}_{p},&p=3,\\ 0.6\,\mathbf{1}_{p},&p=10.\end{cases}

The smaller coefficient magnitude in the p=10p=10 setting offsets the increase in the number of instruments, which controls the first-stage signal strength (SNRD\mathrm{SNR}_{D}) broadly comparable across p=3p=3 and p=10p=10. σZ2=0.075\sigma_{Z}^{2}=0.075 in the 2D design and σZ2=0.108\sigma_{Z}^{2}=0.108 in the 3D design.

Let q=⌊p/2⌋+1q=\lfloor p/2\rfloor+1. The first qq instruments are locally invalid and share the same nonzero effect over a specified region ℛα⊂Ω\mathcal{R}_{\alpha}\subset\Omega; the remaining instruments are valid over the full domain. Thus, q=2q=2 for p=3p=3 and q=6q=6 for p=10p=10. Because the locally invalid instruments form the largest ratio group on ℛα\mathcal{R}_{\alpha}, pointwise plurality fails on that region.

The subject-level spatial error is generated from a finite Karhunen–Loève expansion,

ηi​(𝒔)=∑t=1Tρt1/2​ζi​t​ψt​(𝒔),\eta_{i}(\bm{s})=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\rho_{t}^{1/2}\zeta_{it}\psi_{t}(\bm{s}),

and the measurement errors are independent with εi​(𝒔j)​∼iid​N​(0,σ2)\varepsilon_{i}(\bm{s}_{j})\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^{2}).

The variables {εi​(𝒔j)}\{\varepsilon_{i}(\bm{s}_{j})\} are independent of (𝒁i,ξi,ζi​1,…,ζi​T)(\bm{Z}_{i},\xi_{i},\zeta_{i1},\ldots,\zeta_{iT}). Dependence between ηi​(⋅)\eta_{i}(\cdot) and ξi\xi_{i} induces unmeasured confounding.

Let Ω=[0,1]2\Omega=[0,1]^{2}, with N=95×79=7,505N=95\times 79=7{,}505 equally spaced pixels, and write 𝒔=(s1,s2)⊤\bm{s}=(s_{1},s_{2})^{\top}. The causal-effect function is

ηi​(𝒔)=ρ11/2​ζi​1​ψ1​(𝒔)+ρ21/2​ζi​2​ψ2​(𝒔),\eta_{i}(\bm{s})=\rho_{1}^{1/2}\zeta_{i1}\psi_{1}(\bm{s})+\rho_{2}^{1/2}\zeta_{i2}\psi_{2}(\bm{s}),

where ψ1​(𝒔)=1.42​sin⁡(2​π​s1)\psi_{1}(\bm{s})=1.42\sin(2\pi s_{1}) and ψ2​(𝒔)=1.40​cos⁡(2​π​s2)\psi_{2}(\bm{s})=1.40\cos(2\pi s_{2}). We generate

(ζi​1,ζi​2,ξi)⊤∼N⁡(𝟎,(100.3010.30.30.31)).(\zeta_{i1},\zeta_{i2},\xi_{i})^{\top}\sim N\!\left(\bm{0},\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0.3\\ 0&1&0.3\\ 0.3&0.3&1\end{pmatrix}\right).

For ℓ=1,…,q\ell=1,\ldots,q,

αℓ∗​(𝒔)=4​I​(𝒔∈ℛsm),ℛsm=ℛsq∪ℛcir,\alpha_{\ell}^{\ast}(\bm{s})=4I(\bm{s}\in\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{sm}}),\qquad\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{sm}}=\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{sq}}\cup\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{cir}},

where ℛsq=[0.10,0.30]×[0.68,0.88]\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{sq}}=[0.10,0.30]\times[0.68,0.88] and ℛcir={𝒔∈Ω:(s1−0.82)2+(s2−0.35)2≤0.102}\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{cir}}=\left\{\bm{s}\in\Omega:(s_{1}-0.82)^{2}+(s_{2}-0.35)^{2}\leq 0.10^{2}\right\}. That is, ℛsq\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{sq}} (shown in Figure C.1) is a square centered at (0.22,0.20)(0.22,0.20) with side length 0.200.20, whereas ℛcir\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{cir}} is a disk centered at (0.65,0.82)(0.65,0.82) with radius 0.100.10. For ℓ=q+1,…,p\ell=q+1,\ldots,p, αℓ∗​(𝒔)=0\alpha_{\ell}^{\ast}(\bm{s})=0 on Ω\Omega.

The low- and high-noise settings are

(σ,ρ1,ρ2)={(0.8,0.1,0.1),low noise,(1.5,0.2,0.2),high noise.(\sigma,\rho_{1},\rho_{2})=\begin{cases}(0.8,0.1,0.1),&\text{low noise},\\ (1.5,0.2,0.2),&\text{high noise}.\end{cases}

β∗​(𝒔)=3.5​I​(𝒔∈𝒬)+{3​(s1+0.2)2−(s2+0.2)2}​I​(𝒔∉𝒬).\beta^{\ast}(\bm{s})=3.5\,I(\bm{s}\in\mathcal{Q})+\{3(s_{1}+0.2)^{2}-(s_{2}+0.2)^{2}\}I(\bm{s}\notin\mathcal{Q}).

For the spatially adaptive fit, the square domain is partitioned into the following four rectangular subdomains:

Ω1\displaystyle\Omega_{1} =[0,0.6]×[0,0.6],\displaystyle=[0,0.6]\times[0,0.6], Ω2\displaystyle\Omega_{2} =[0.6,1.0]×[0,0.6],\displaystyle=[0.6,1.0]\times[0,0.6],

ℛ2\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{2} =[0.750,0.875]×[0.750,0.875]×[0.625,0.875],\displaystyle=[0.750,0.875]\times[0.750,0.875]\times[0.625,0.875],

(σ,ρ1,ρ2,ρ3)={(1.5,0.20,0.02,0.01),low noise,(3.0,0.50,0.05,0.02),high noise.(\sigma,\rho_{1},\rho_{2},\rho_{3})=\begin{cases}(1.5,0.20,0.02,0.01),&\text{low noise},\\ (3.0,0.50,0.05,0.02),&\text{high noise}.\end{cases}

C.2 Signal-to-noise ratios

We characterize the simulation settings using two signal-to-noise ratios. The first-stage signal-to-noise ratio,

SNRD=Var⁡(𝐙⊤​𝜸∗)Var⁡(ξ),\mathrm{SNR}_{D}=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(\mathbf{Z}^{\top}\bm{\gamma}^{\ast})}{\operatorname{Var}(\xi)}, (C.1)

quantifies the strength of the candidate instruments. The imaging signal-to-noise ratio is defined as

SNRY=N−1​∑j=1NVar⁡[Di​β∗​(𝐬j)+∑ℓ=1pZi​ℓ​αℓ∗​(𝐬j)]N−1​∑j=1NVar⁡{ηi​(𝒔j)+εi​(𝐬j)},\mathrm{SNR}_{Y}=\frac{N^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\operatorname{Var}\left[D_{i}\beta^{\ast}(\mathbf{s}_{j})+\sum_{\ell=1}^{p}Z_{i\ell}\alpha^{\ast}_{\ell}(\mathbf{s}_{j})\right]}{N^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\operatorname{Var}\left\{\eta_{i}(\bm{s}_{j})+\varepsilon_{i}(\mathbf{s}_{j})\right\}}, (C.2)

which measures the average signal strength of the imaging outcome relative to the observation noise. Throughout the simulations, we report both SNRD\mathrm{SNR}_{D} and SNRY\mathrm{SNR}_{Y} to distinguish the effects of instrument strength and imaging noise. The realized SNR values among all scenarios are reported in Table C.3.

C.3 Implementation and tuning

Hi-FIVE represents β⁡(⋅)\beta(\cdot) and αℓ​(⋅)\alpha_{\ell}(\cdot) using Bernstein–Bézier splines over nested triangulations △1\triangle_{1} and △2\triangle_{2}, respectively, where △2\triangle_{2} is obtained by uniform refinement of △1\triangle_{1}. In two dimensions, each parent triangle is divided into four subtriangles; in three dimensions, each parent tetrahedron is divided into eight subtetrahedra. Locations lying exactly on shared edges or faces are removed when constructing local basis matrices to avoid duplicate simplex assignments.

For each candidate λR\lambda^{\rm R}, a solution path over λS\lambda^{\rm S} is fitted and λS\lambda^{\rm S} is selected by mBIC. The final λR\lambda^{\rm R} is selected by subject-level KK-fold cross-validation. The optimization uses local linear approximation for the nonconvex group penalty, coordinate updates for the instrument–simplex blocks, and consensus ADMM for the continuity constraints on β⁡(⋅)\beta(\cdot).

Across implementations, the numerical implementation uses a maximum of 20 outer LLA iterations and 100 inner coordinate-descent passes. The LLA, coordinate-descent, and ADMM convergence tolerances are 10−410^{-4}; the ADMM penalty is 22 with a maximum of 10310^{3} ADMM iterations and 10310^{3} conjugate-gradient iterations. The sparsity path is set to 60 logarithmically spaced values, decreasing from 10310^{3} to 10−610^{-6} in the 2D case and from e−1.5e^{-1.5} to e−5e^{-5} in the 3D case.

C.4 Evaluation criteria

For Monte Carlo replication r=1,…,Rr=1,\ldots,R, define

ISE(r)=1N​∑j=1N{β^(r)​(𝒔j)−β∗​(𝒔j)}2.\operatorname{ISE}^{(r)}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\{\widehat{\beta}^{(r)}(\bm{s}_{j})-\beta^{\ast}(\bm{s}_{j})\}^{2}.

We report

MISE=1R​∑r=1RISE(r),SDISE=[1R−1​∑r=1R{ISE(r)−MISE}2]1/2.\operatorname{MISE}=\frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^{R}\operatorname{ISE}^{(r)},\qquad\operatorname{SD}_{\mathrm{ISE}}=\left[\frac{1}{R-1}\sum_{r=1}^{R}\{\operatorname{ISE}^{(r)}-\operatorname{MISE}\}^{2}\right]^{1/2}.

For a nominal simultaneous confidence level 1−τ1-\tau, the empirical coverage rate is ECR=1R​∑r=1RI⁡{β∗​(𝒔j)∈𝒞^1−τ(r)​(𝒔j),j=1,…,N}.\operatorname{ECR}=\frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^{R}I\left\{\beta^{\ast}(\bm{s}_{j})\in\widehat{\mathcal{C}}^{(r)}_{1-\tau}(\bm{s}_{j}),\ j=1,\ldots,N\right\}.

C.5 Additional estimation results

Illustration: comparison of estimators for the 3D smooth case

C.6 Triangulation sensitivity

The smooth two-dimensional design with n=300n=300 and p=10p=10 is fitted using coarse, default, and fine triangulations. In addition, the interior vertices of the default triangulation are independently perturbed while preserving the domain boundary and mesh validity. All estimates are evaluated on the common pixel/voxel grid.

The triangulation sensitivity analysis shows that the Hi-FIVE estimator is generally stable across reasonable mesh resolutions. The coarse and default triangulations yield nearly identical MISE and variability for both p=3p=3 and p=10p=10, indicating that the estimation results are not sensitive to moderate changes in the number of simplices. Under low noise, the fine triangulation also produces comparable performance. Under high noise, the fine mesh results in a slight increase in MISE. Additionally, the corresponding standard deviations remain similar across the three resolutions. Thus, further refinement beyond the default mesh provides little additional benefit. Overall, these results indicate that Hi-FIVE is robust to the choice of triangulation within a practical range, while the default mesh resolution provides a favorable balance between approximation accuracy and estimation stability.

Section D. Additional Details for Application

Covariate adjustment

Age, sex, and diagnosis are included as adjustment covariates. Age is standardized, sex is coded as female versus male, and diagnosis is coded as cognitively normal (CN) versus cognitively impaired (EMCI/MCI). To adjust for these covariates, we residualize the imaging outcome, p-tau exposure, and genetic instruments with respect to age, sex, and diagnosis prior to estimation. The subsequent first-stage regression and Hi-FIVE analysis are performed using the resulting residualized variables.

Implementation details

For the real-data analysis, we use a triangulation consisting of K1=317K_{1}=317 tetrahedra for modeling the spatially varying causal effect. The same triangulation is used to define the subregions for the invalid-IV effects, yielding K2=317K_{2}=317. The spline degree and smoothness pairs are (d1,r1)=(5,1)(d_{1},r_{1})=(5,1) for β\beta and (d2,r2)=(5,0)(d_{2},r_{2})=(5,0) for each αℓ\alpha_{\ell}. The first-stage SNR is 0.176. We use a maximum of 20 outer LLA iterations and 100 inner coordinate-descent passes. The LLA, coordinate-descent, and ADMM convergence tolerances are all set to 10−410^{-4}, with an ADMM penalty parameter of 2, a maximum of 10310^{3} ADMM iterations, and 10310^{3} conjugate-gradient iterations. The smoothing parameter grid ranges from 10110^{1} to 10−710^{-7}, while the sparsity parameter is selected over a path of 30 logarithmically spaced values decreasing from e−1e^{-1} to e−7e^{-7}.

Invalid IV illustration

The IV effects for five SNPs (rs744373, rs3820757, rs11136000, rs6656401 and rs3851179) are shown in Figure C.5. The colored regions represent the estimated nonzero invalid-IV effects, with blue indicating negative signals and orange to red indicating positive signals. Overall, the invalid-IV effects are sparse and spatially clustered, with clear SNP-specific patterns: rs744373 and rs3820757 show mainly positive clusters, whereas rs11136000 shows a smaller mixed pattern with both negative and positive regions. In contrast, rs6656401 and rs3851179 show predominantly negative clusters. Across the right lateral and superior views, these effects remain spatially localized, supporting the use of spatially varying invalid-IV estimation in the Hi-FIVE analysis.
